practices.title: Empty catch block swallows exceptions
practices.description: Catching an exception and doing nothing hides failures until they surface somewhere confusing much later, instead of at the point they actually happened.
practices.risk: Data corruption or a broken downstream call goes unnoticed; the bug report that eventually comes in points nowhere near the real cause.

practices.title: Catching generic Exception instead of a specific type
practices.description: Catching Exception or Throwable masks unrelated failures, including unchecked bugs like a NullPointerException, as if they were the expected failure mode.
practices.risk: A real bug (NPE, ClassCastException) gets silently absorbed by handling meant for an expected, recoverable failure like a missing file.
practices.detectionPattern: catch\s*\(\s*(Exception|Throwable)\s+\w+\s*\)

practices.title: Losing the original exception cause when wrapping
practices.description: Wrapping an exception in a new one without passing the original as the cause discards the stack trace that shows what actually failed.
practices.risk: Production incident logs show only the wrapper's generic message; diagnosing the real failure requires reproducing it from scratch.
practices.detectionPattern: throw\s+new\s+\w+Exception\("[^"]*"\)\s*;

practices.title: Throwing a generic RuntimeException with a vague message
practices.description: A bare RuntimeException("Error") tells the caller and the operator nothing about what went wrong or how to react to it.
practices.risk: An on-call engineer paged at 3am sees only 'Error' in the stack trace and has to read the surrounding code to find out what actually failed.
practices.detectionPattern: throw\s+new\s+(RuntimeException|Exception)\("(Error|Failed|Something went wrong)"\)

practices.title: Catching NullPointerException or ClassCastException as control flow
practices.description: NullPointerException and ClassCastException almost always indicate a programming bug, not an expected condition to branch on.
practices.risk: The actual bug (why the reference was null) is hidden behind a catch block that treats the crash as normal, so it never gets fixed and can resurface with worse consequences elsewhere.
practices.detectionPattern: catch\s*\(\s*(NullPointerException|ClassCastException)\s+\w+\s*\)

practices.title: Catching an exception just to wrap and rethrow it as the same type with no added value
practices.description: A catch block that immediately wraps an exception in a new instance of the same (or an equally generic) type, without adding context, translating to a different abstraction level, or performing any recovery, only adds noise and an extra stack frame.
practices.risk: The extra catch-wrap-rethrow adds a stack frame and a line of code that does nothing but obscure that the original exception was already fine to propagate as-is.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: catch blocks whose only action is `throw new SameOrEquallyGenericException(message, e)` with no new contextual information.

practices.title: Exception messages with no contextual information
practices.description: A message like "Error occurred" or "Invalid input" gives on-call engineers nothing to act on.
practices.risk: Including the relevant identifiers, values, or operation name turns a stack trace into an actionable lead.
practices.code: throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid input"); // which input? what was invalid about it?
practices.solution:
throw new IllegalArgumentException(
    "Order quantity must be positive, but was " + quantity + " for order " + orderId);
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Exception constructors called with short, generic literal strings ('Error', 'Invalid input', 'Failed') containing no variables from the surrounding context.

practices.title: Ignoring suppressed exceptions from try-with-resources
practices.description: When both the try block and an automatic resource-close() throw, the close() exception is attached as a 'suppressed' exception rather than replacing the primary one.
practices.risk: Code that only logs e.getMessage() silently drops this second failure, which can hide a real resource-cleanup bug.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: catch blocks around try-with-resources that log only e.getMessage() and never inspect e.getSuppressed().

practices.title: Catching an exception and returning null instead of propagating or handling it explicitly
practices.description: Converting a failure into a null return value moves the problem to every caller, who must now remember to null-check, and the original exception's context (type, message, stack trace) is completely lost.
practices.risk: The caller has no way to tell a genuine error apart from a legitimate 'not found', and the original exception's type, message, and stack trace are gone.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: catch blocks whose body is exactly `return null;` with no logging or rethrow, especially where the method's normal (non-error) result could also be null or empty.

practices.title: Throwing an exception from a finally block, suppressing the original exception from the try block
practices.description: If both the try block and its finally block throw, only the finally block's exception propagates — the original exception (often the more informative one) is silently discarded with no trace of it ever having occurred.
practices.risk: The finally block's exception silently replaces the try block's original exception, so the caller never learns what actually failed first.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: finally blocks containing code that can throw (especially resource cleanup) with no internal try/catch to prevent it from replacing an in-flight exception from the try block.

practices.title: Logging and swallowing an exception while continuing execution as if it succeeded
practices.description: Logging an exception is better than an empty catch block, but if execution proceeds normally afterward with no fallback or state correction, the program continues operating on data or state it knows is invalid, which is often worse than failing loudly.
practices.risk: The program continues operating on data it knows is wrong (an order marked complete when its stock was never actually decremented), which is often worse than failing loudly.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: catch blocks that log the exception but whose enclosing method continues to the same success path it would have taken without a failure, without an explicit compensating action.

practices.title: Combining unrelated exception types in a single multi-catch block that need different handling
practices.description: Java's multi-catch (catch (A | B e)) is meant for exceptions that genuinely deserve identical handling.
practices.risk: Grouping unrelated exception types together just to reduce code duplication means at least one of them ends up mishandled, since the shared block can't tailor its response to each.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Multi-catch blocks whose exception types have no common recovery strategy in the block body (e.g. one is retried, the other logically shouldn't be).

practices.title: Letting low-level exceptions leak across architectural layers instead of translating them
practices.description: Allowing a persistence-layer exception like SQLException or a specific HTTP client exception to propagate all the way up to the service or presentation layer couples unrelated layers to implementation details and makes it impossible to swap the underlying technology without changing unrelated code.
practices.risk: The service or presentation layer becomes coupled to a persistence/network implementation detail, and swapping that underlying technology later requires changing unrelated layers.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Method signatures in service/controller layers declaring throws clauses for, or directly propagating, exception types owned by a lower persistence/network layer.

practices.title: Giving custom exceptions mutable state, making them unsafe to reuse or share
practices.description: Exception instances are often passed across thread boundaries (logged asynchronously, stored for later inspection, rethrown by multiple callers).
practices.risk: Mutable fields on a custom exception invite the same shared-mutable-state bugs as any other object, but are easy to overlook because exceptions 'feel' like one-shot, disposable values.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Custom exception classes with non-final mutable fields or setter-style methods that mutate state after construction.

practices.title: Attempting to catch and 'recover' from Error/OutOfMemoryError
practices.description: Throwable subclasses under Error (OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError, VirtualMachineError) signal conditions the JVM itself may no longer be able to guarantee correct behavior for.
practices.risk: Catching them and trying to continue normal operation risks running in a corrupted or unpredictable state instead of failing safely.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: catch (Error e) or catch (OutOfMemoryError e) / catch (StackOverflowError e) blocks whose code path continues normal business logic afterward instead of failing fast or shutting down.

practices.title: Retrying an operation on exception without backoff or a maximum retry limit
practices.description: An unconditional retry loop that immediately retries on failure with no cap and no delay can turn a transient blip into a self-inflicted denial-of-service against the downstream dependency, and never terminates if the failure is actually permanent.
practices.risk: An unconditional, immediate retry loop can turn a transient blip into a self-inflicted denial-of-service against the downstream dependency, and never terminates if the failure is actually permanent.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Retry loops around a fallible call with no attempt counter/max-retries condition and no delay between attempts.

practices.title: Catching one exception type and throwing an unrelated exception type that breaks the caller's expected contract
practices.description: If a method's documented/declared exceptions are IOException-related but a catch block translates a failure into, say, an unrelated NumberFormatException, callers who catch by the documented type miss it entirely, and it surfaces as an unhandled failure somewhere unrelated to where it actually occurred.
practices.risk: A global error handler that maps exception types to HTTP status codes can't reliably distinguish a user-facing business rule violation from an infrastructure failure, since both extend the same generic type.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: catch blocks that throw an exception type unrelated to the method's declared throws clause or documented exception contract.

practices.title: Using instanceof chains on caught exceptions instead of exception-type polymorphism
practices.description: Catching a broad exception type and then branching on instanceof for each specific subtype re-implements what multiple catch clauses (or a proper exception hierarchy with a handle() method) already do at the language level, and is easy to get wrong as new exception subtypes are added without updating every instanceof chain.
practices.risk: Adding a new exception subtype means finding and updating every instanceof chain by hand, with no compiler error to catch a chain that was missed.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: catch (Exception e) blocks whose body is a chain of if (e instanceof X) checks that could instead be separate catch clauses.

practices.title: Not setting the cause when constructing a custom wrapping exception
practices.description: Custom exceptions that only take a message (and drop the original exception) break the cause chain
practices.risk: the stack trace shows only where the new exception was thrown, not the underlying root cause that triggered it.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_ANNOTATION_HEURISTIC: new CustomException(message) inside a catch block where the caught exception variable is available but never passed as the constructor's second argument (cause)

practices.title: Defining a custom exception class that adds no fields or behavior over an existing standard exception
practices.description: Creating OrderException extends RuntimeException with only a message constructor and nothing else duplicates what IllegalStateException or IllegalArgumentException already provide, adding a class to maintain without adding any real capability (extra fields, custom methods, distinct catchability that matters).
practices.risk: Adds a class to maintain that offers no real capability over the standard exception it duplicates, with no distinct catchability or extra data to justify it.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: custom exception class whose entire body is a pass-through message-only constructor with no additional fields or methods

practices.title: Calling System.exit() from within exception-handling code in application or library logic
practices.description: System.exit() terminates the entire JVM immediately, bypassing normal exception propagation, finally blocks in other threads, shutdown hooks that haven't registered, and any caller's ability to decide how to respond
practices.risk: it's rarely appropriate outside of a dedicated top-level main() failure path.

practices.title: Catching NullPointerException defensively instead of adding an explicit null check
practices.description: Wrapping code in try/catch (NullPointerException e) to guard against a possibly-null value hides exactly where the null came from and treats a preventable programming error the same as an unpredictable runtime condition
practices.risk: an explicit check documents the expectation and fails at the real source.
practices.solution:
Address address = customer.getAddress();
return (address != null) ? address.getCity() : "Unknown"; // explicit, self-documenting, and doesn't mask an unrelated NPE elsewhere in the expression
practices.detectionPattern: catch\s*\(\s*NullPointerException\s+\w+\s*\)

practices.title: Returning null instead of Optional or an empty collection
practices.description: A null return forces every caller to remember a null check or risk an NPE far from the source. An empty List/Optional makes the absent case impossible to forget.
practices.risk: A caller that forgets the null check throws an NPE in production, often several layers away from where null originated.
practices.detectionPattern: return\s+null\s*;

practices.title: Returning null instead of an empty array
practices.description: Effective Java Item 54: a null array return forces every caller to add a null check that's easy to forget, mirroring the same problem as a null collection return.
practices.risk: A caller that iterates the result without a null check throws an NPE; this is especially easy to miss because arrays look like they should never be null.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: array-returning method with a null branch instead of an empty array

practices.title: String compared with == instead of .equals()
practices.description: == compares object identity, not content. Two equal strings from different sources (e.g. one from a DB read) can be == false while .equals() correctly returns true.
practices.risk: A conditional silently takes the wrong branch whenever the string wasn't interned the same way, e.g. after deserialization or string concatenation.

practices.title: Overriding equals() without hashCode() (or vice versa)
practices.description: Effective Java Item 11: equal objects must have equal hashCodes. Overriding one without the other breaks that contract.
practices.risk: The object is silently lost in a HashMap/HashSet: put() and get() with an 'equal' key can disagree on whether the entry exists, because they land in different hash buckets.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: class overrides equals() but not hashCode(), or vice versa

practices.title: Comparing floating-point numbers with ==
practices.description: Floating-point arithmetic is imprecise; two values that are mathematically equal can differ in their last bits after a computation.
practices.risk: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 evaluates to false in Java, so a guard relying on exact float/double equality silently takes the wrong branch.
practices.detectionPattern: double\s+\w+.*==\s*\d+\.\d+

practices.title: == on boxed types relying on autoboxing cache
practices.description: Integer/Long caching only covers -128 to 127. Two boxed values in that range can be == true by accident, creating a false impression that == works for boxed comparison.
practices.risk: Code that 'works' in testing with small numbers (e.g. quantities 1-10) breaks in production once a real value like 1000 is compared, because it falls outside the cache range.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: == comparison between two Integer/Long-typed variables

practices.title: Closeable resource opened without try-with-resources
practices.description: A stream/connection opened without try-with-resources leaks a file handle or connection if the code between open and close throws.
practices.risk: Under load, leaked file handles or DB connections exhaust the pool and the whole service starts failing unrelated requests.
practices.detectionPattern: new\s+(FileInputStream|FileOutputStream|BufferedReader|FileReader)\([^)]*\)\s*;

practices.title: Relying on finalize() for cleanup
practices.description: finalize() is deprecated since Java 9, runs at an unpredictable time (or never), and was never a reliable cleanup mechanism.
practices.risk: A file handle or connection 'cleaned up' only in finalize() may stay open far longer than expected, or forever if the GC never collects the object, exhausting a limited resource pool.
practices.detectionPattern: protected\s+void\s+finalize\s*\(

practices.title: Not closing AutoCloseable streams returned by Files.lines()/Files.list()
practices.description: Files.lines() and Files.list() open an underlying file handle/directory stream that must be closed.
practices.risk: Unlike in-memory streams, these implement AutoCloseable and leak file descriptors if not used in a try-with-resources block.
practices.code:
Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(path);
lines.forEach(System.out::println); // file handle never closed
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Files.lines()/Files.list()/Files.walk() results assigned to a variable and used outside a try-with-resources block.

practices.title: Mutable HashMap shared across threads without synchronization
practices.description: HashMap is not thread-safe. Concurrent reads/writes from multiple threads can corrupt its internal structure or return stale/incorrect data.
practices.risk: Under concurrent load this can infinite-loop a thread (classic HashMap resize bug) or silently drop/return wrong entries — both hard to reproduce outside production traffic.
practices.code: private final Map<String, Session> sessions = new HashMap<>();
practices.solution: private final Map<String, Session> sessions = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
practices.detectionPattern: new\s+HashMap<[^>]*>\(\)

practices.title: Swallowing InterruptedException without restoring interrupt status
practices.description: Catching InterruptedException and doing nothing (or just logging) clears the thread's interrupt flag, so code further up the call stack that checks for cancellation never finds out.
practices.risk: A thread pool shutdown or task cancellation silently fails to stop this thread's work, because the interrupt signal was absorbed and never propagated.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: catch (InterruptedException e) block that doesn't call Thread.currentThread().interrupt()

practices.title: Forgetting lock.unlock() in a finally block
practices.description: Unlike synchronized, an explicit Lock is not automatically released. If the code between lock() and unlock() throws, and unlock() isn't in a finally block, the lock is held forever.
practices.risk: One exception permanently deadlocks every other thread that needs the same lock, with no exception or log pointing at the actual cause.

practices.title: Calling run() instead of start() on a Thread
practices.description: run() executes the Runnable's code on the current thread, synchronously. It does not create or start a new thread — only start() does that.
practices.risk: Code that looks concurrent (spawns a Thread, calls a method on it) actually runs entirely sequentially on the calling thread; any expected parallelism silently never happens.
practices.code:
Thread t = new Thread(() -> doWork());
t.run();  // runs in the calling thread!

practices.title: Relying on Thread.stop(), Thread.suspend(), or Thread.resume()
practices.description: These methods are deprecated because they're inherently unsafe: stop() can release locks mid-update and leave shared objects in a corrupted, half-modified state.
practices.risk: A thread killed via stop() mid-write can leave a shared data structure permanently corrupted, with no exception raised to indicate anything went wrong.
practices.code:
thread.stop();
thread.suspend();
practices.solution:
thread.interrupt();
// or a higher-level construct: ExecutorService.shutdownNow(), Future.cancel()
practices.detectionPattern: \.(stop|suspend|resume)\(\)\s*;

practices.title: Iterating a Collections.synchronizedList() without external synchronization
practices.description: Collections.synchronizedXxx() wrappers make individual method calls thread-safe, but iteration is not atomic.
practices.risk: Iterating without synchronizing on the collection itself can still throw ConcurrentModificationException if another thread mutates it mid-iteration.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: for-each loops over a Collections.synchronizedXxx() collection with no surrounding synchronized(collection) block.

practices.title: Non-atomic get-check-put pattern on ConcurrentHashMap instead of computeIfAbsent()/merge()
practices.description: Checking containsKey()/get() and then calling put() as separate steps is not atomic.
practices.risk: Two threads can interleave between the check and the write, causing lost updates or duplicate initialization, even on a thread-safe map implementation.
practices.solution:
cache.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> expensiveCompute(k)); // atomic check-and-set
// Or cache.merge(key, value, (old, v) -> combine(old, v)) for combining updates
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: containsKey()/get() followed by a conditional put() on a ConcurrentHashMap (or any map shared across threads) instead of a single atomic compute-family call.

practices.title: Not clearing MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) values between requests in thread-pooled environments
practices.description: MDC stores per-thread key-value pairs (like a request/trace ID) that get included in every log line.
practices.risk: In a thread pool where threads are reused across requests, forgetting to clear the MDC at the end of a request lets its values leak into the logs of the next, unrelated request handled by the same thread.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: MDC.put() calls not paired with a corresponding MDC.remove()/MDC.clear() inside a finally block, in code running on a reused thread (servlet/executor thread pools).

practices.title: Synchronizing on a lock object whose reference can change
practices.description: synchronized(lock) locks on whatever object 'lock' currently refers to
practices.risk: if that field is non-final and gets reassigned, different threads can end up synchronizing on different objects entirely, providing no mutual exclusion at all.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_ANNOTATION_HEURISTIC: field used as a synchronized() lock target that is not declared final, or is reassigned elsewhere in the class

practices.title: Double-checked locking without a volatile field
practices.description: The double-checked locking idiom for lazy singleton initialization only works correctly if the field is volatile
practices.risk: without it, another thread can observe a partially-constructed object due to instruction reordering, even though the null-check appears to pass after the object was 'assigned'.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_ANNOTATION_HEURISTIC: double-checked locking pattern (null-check, synchronized, null-check, assign) on a field not declared volatile

practices.title: Using Thread.sleep() as a substitute for proper synchronization or coordination
practices.description: Sleeping for a guessed duration to 'wait until another thread is probably done' is inherently racy
practices.risk: the actual work might take longer under load, or finish sooner, wasting time; proper coordination primitives (CountDownLatch, CompletableFuture, join()) wait exactly as long as needed and no longer.
practices.solution:
CompletableFuture<Result> future = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(this::backgroundTask);
Result result = future.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // waits exactly as long as needed, with an explicit timeout ceiling
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Thread.sleep() used to wait for another thread's work to complete rather than genuine backoff/rate limiting

practices.title: Not shutting down an ExecutorService, leaking threads
practices.description: An ExecutorService's threads are not daemon threads by default
practices.risk: if it's never shutdown()/shutdownNow(), those threads (and the executor itself) stay alive indefinitely, leaking resources and, for a standalone application, preventing the JVM from exiting.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: ExecutorService created with no corresponding shutdown()/shutdownNow() call anywhere in its owning class

practices.title: Not removing a ThreadLocal value after use in a pooled-thread environment
practices.description: In an application server or executor thread pool, threads are reused across many requests/tasks
practices.risk: a ThreadLocal value set during one request but never removed persists into the next request handled by the same thread, leaking data (and potentially sensitive information) between unrelated requests.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: ThreadLocal.set() in request/task-scoped code with no matching remove() in a finally block

practices.title: Using wait() without a loop that re-checks the condition, ignoring spurious wakeups
practices.description: The Java memory model permits a thread to wake up from wait() even without a matching notify() (a 'spurious wakeup'), and multiple waiting threads can also be woken by one notifyAll() and race to re-check state
practices.risk: wait() must always be called inside a while loop that re-verifies the condition, not a plain if.

practices.title: Running blocking synchronized code inside a virtual thread, causing platform-thread pinning
practices.description: Virtual threads (Java 21+) normally unmount from their carrier platform thread while blocked on I/O, freeing that platform thread for other work
practices.risk: however, a virtual thread blocked inside a synchronized block or native method stays pinned to its carrier thread for the block's duration, which can exhaust the limited platform-thread pool under high concurrency.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: synchronized block or method performing blocking I/O internally, executed on a virtual thread

practices.title: Creating unbounded thread pools or one raw Thread per task
practices.description: Executors.newUnboundedXxx()-style pools (like newCachedThreadPool()) and manually spawning a new Thread for every incoming task have no upper bound on concurrent threads
practices.risk: under sustained or bursty load this can exhaust memory (each thread reserves stack space) or overwhelm the OS scheduler.
practices.detectionPattern: new\s+Thread\([^)]*\)\.start\(\)|Executors\.newCachedThreadPool\(

practices.title: Reading/writing a shared field with no synchronization or volatile, relying on unguaranteed visibility
practices.description: Without synchronization, volatile, or another Java Memory Model happens-before mechanism, one thread's write to a shared field is not guaranteed to ever become visible to another thread reading it
practices.risk: the reading thread may loop forever on a stale cached value, even though the field 'looks' correctly updated in a debugger.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_ANNOTATION_HEURISTIC: boolean/int field read by one thread and written by another that is not volatile, not synchronized, and not an AtomicXxx type

practices.title: Calling CompletableFuture.get() without a timeout
practices.description: The no-argument get() blocks indefinitely if the future never completes (e.g. the async task hangs or its underlying dependency never responds)
practices.risk: supplying a timeout ensures the calling thread eventually gives up and the caller can react instead of hanging forever.
practices.code: Result result = future.get(); // blocks forever if the async computation never completes
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: CompletableFuture.get()/Future.get() called with no timeout arguments

practices.title: Acquiring multiple locks in inconsistent order across different code paths
practices.description: If thread A locks resource X then Y, while thread B locks Y then X, the two threads can each acquire one lock and then block forever waiting for the other
practices.risk: a classic deadlock. Consistently ordering lock acquisition everywhere in the codebase prevents this class of bug entirely.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: nested synchronized/lock acquisitions on the same set of objects with inconsistent ordering across call sites

practices.title: Wrapping already-atomic operations in redundant external synchronization
practices.description: AtomicInteger/AtomicLong/etc. already guarantee atomicity for operations like incrementAndGet() internally (via CAS)
practices.risk: wrapping a call to them in an additional synchronized block adds contention and complexity without improving correctness.
practices.solution:
private final AtomicInteger counter = new AtomicInteger();
counter.incrementAndGet(); // atomicity already guaranteed, no external lock needed
practices.detectionPattern: synchronized\s*\([^)]*\)\s*\{\s*\w+\.(?:incrementAndGet|decrementAndGet|getAndIncrement|getAndSet|addAndGet|compareAndSet)\([^;]*\);\s*\}

practices.title: Busy-spin waiting without backoff, wasting CPU while making no progress
practices.description: A tight while loop that repeatedly checks a condition with no yield, sleep, or backoff pins a CPU core at 100% and starves other threads of scheduling time, all while making no forward progress itself
practices.risk: worse than blocking, which lets the scheduler give the core to useful work.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: while loop polling a shared condition with no Thread.sleep()/yield()/onSpinWait() call in its body

practices.title: Sharing a single java.util.Random instance across threads instead of ThreadLocalRandom
practices.description: java.util.Random is thread-safe but internally synchronizes on a single seed field
practices.risk: concurrent calls from many threads serialize and become a contention bottleneck; ThreadLocalRandom gives each thread its own generator with no shared state or locking.
practices.detectionPattern: (?:private|public|protected)?\s*(?:static\s+)?(?:final\s+)?Random\s+\w+\s*=\s*new\s+Random\(\)

practices.title: Using coarse-grained synchronized methods on hot-path objects instead of finer-grained locking
practices.description: Synchronizing an entire method (or a large block covering unrelated fields) on a frequently-called object serializes all access to it, even between operations that don't actually conflict
practices.risk: splitting locks by the data they actually protect (or using lock-free/concurrent structures) reduces contention significantly under load.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: synchronized method on a high-call-volume class whose body touches independent fields that don't need to be serialized together

practices.title: Starting a thread from within a constructor before the object is fully constructed
practices.description: If a constructor starts a thread that calls back into the object being constructed (e.g. via 'this'), the new thread can observe a partially-initialized instance
practices.risk: fields set after the Thread.start() call may not yet be assigned when the new thread begins running, a classic 'this' escape bug.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_ANNOTATION_HEURISTIC: Thread.start()/executor.submit() inside a constructor passing 'this' or a method reference bound to 'this'

practices.title: Using notify() instead of notifyAll() when multiple threads may be waiting for different conditions
practices.description: notify() wakes an arbitrary single thread waiting on the monitor
practices.risk: if several threads are waiting for different conditions on the same lock, notify() might wake a thread whose condition still isn't met, leaving the thread that actually could have proceeded still asleep — a missed-wakeup bug.
practices.detectionPattern: \bnotify\(\)

practices.title: Assuming ConcurrentHashMap.size()/isEmpty() are exact, consistent point-in-time snapshots
practices.description: size() and isEmpty() on ConcurrentHashMap are approximations designed to avoid locking the whole map
practices.risk: under concurrent modification, the returned value may be stale by the time the caller acts on it, so code that treats it as an exact count can make incorrect decisions.

practices.title: Reusing a CountDownLatch expecting it to reset for a new round of coordination
practices.description: A CountDownLatch's counter can only ever count down to zero once
practices.risk: it cannot be reset or reused for a subsequent round of the same coordination pattern. Code that tries to 'reuse' one for repeated phases either needs a fresh latch each time or should use CyclicBarrier, which is designed to reset automatically.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: a single CountDownLatch instance referenced across more than one logical round of coordination

practices.title: Submitting tasks via ExecutorService.execute() and letting uncaught exceptions disappear silently
practices.description: An exception thrown inside a Runnable submitted via execute() (as opposed to submit()
practices.risk: captures it in the returned Future) is handled by the thread's UncaughtExceptionHandler — by default this just prints to stderr and the failure is otherwise invisible, with no way for the submitting code to know the task failed.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: ExecutorService.execute() (rather than submit()) used for a task whose failure needs to be observed

practices.title: Ignoring the list of unstarted tasks returned by shutdownNow()
practices.description: shutdownNow() attempts to stop all actively executing tasks and returns a List of tasks that were queued but never started
practices.risk: discarding that return value silently drops work that the application may still need to account for, retry, or report as incomplete.
practices.code: executor.shutdownNow(); // queued tasks are simply lost, with no record of what didn't run
practices.detectionPattern: (?<!=\s)\b\w+\.shutdownNow\(\)

practices.title: Assuming shutdown() blocks until all tasks finish instead of calling awaitTermination()
practices.description: shutdown() only stops the executor from accepting new tasks and returns immediately
practices.risk: it does not wait for already-submitted tasks to complete. Code that proceeds right after shutdown() assuming all work is done can read incomplete results or exit the JVM with tasks still mid-execution.
practices.code:
executor.shutdown();
processResults(); // tasks may still be running — shutdown() didn't wait for them
practices.detectionPattern: \.shutdown\(\)\s*;(?![\s\S]{0,200}?awaitTermination)

practices.title: Submitting blocking I/O tasks to the common ForkJoinPool
practices.description: parallelStream() and CompletableFuture's async methods (without an explicit executor) use the shared, JVM-wide common ForkJoinPool by default, sized to the number of CPU cores
practices.risk: submitting long blocking I/O operations to it ties up those few threads and can starve unrelated parallel streams or CompletableFuture chains running elsewhere in the same application.
practices.solution:
ExecutorService ioExecutor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(50); // dedicated pool sized for I/O concurrency
List<CompletableFuture<Result>> futures = list.stream()
    .map(item -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> callSlowExternalApi(item), ioExecutor))
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: blocking I/O invoked inside a parallelStream() pipeline or CompletableFuture async method with no explicit executor

practices.title: Using volatile on a field that undergoes compound read-modify-write operations
practices.description: volatile only guarantees visibility and ordering for individual reads/writes
practices.risk: it does not make a compound operation like increment (read, add one, write) atomic. Two threads can both read the same value before either writes back, losing an update, even though the field is volatile.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_ANNOTATION_HEURISTIC: volatile int/long field modified via ++/--/+=/-= compound assignment instead of AtomicInteger/AtomicLong

practices.title: Using per-business-key lock objects stored in a plain, non-thread-safe Map
practices.description: A common pattern for per-key locking is `locks.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new Object())`, then synchronizing on the returned object
practices.risk: if the backing Map itself isn't thread-safe (or the get-then-create isn't atomic), two threads can each create a different lock instance for the same logical key, giving no real mutual exclusion.
practices.detectionPattern: new\s+HashMap<[^>]*>\s*\(\s*\)\s*;[\s\S]{0,200}?\.computeIfAbsent\([^,]+,\s*\w+\s*->\s*new\s+Object\(\)\)

practices.title: Leaking a mutable internal array or collection through a getter on an otherwise-immutable class
practices.description: A class with all-final fields can still be mutated from the outside if a getter returns the actual internal array/collection reference instead of a defensive copy or unmodifiable view
practices.risk: any thread holding that reference can mutate 'immutable' shared state without synchronization, breaking the safety guarantee the immutability was meant to provide.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: getter on an immutable/thread-safe class returning an internal array or mutable-collection field directly without a defensive copy

practices.title: Lazily initializing a shared, non-thread-safe collection field without synchronization
practices.description: A field initialized on first use with `if (list == null) { list = new ArrayList<>()
practices.risk: }` (with no synchronization) can be initialized twice by two racing threads, each getting a different list instance and silently losing whatever the other thread adds to 'its' copy.
practices.detectionPattern: if\s*\(\s*(\w+)\s*==\s*null\s*\)\s*\{\s*\1\s*=\s*new\s+(?:ArrayList|HashMap|HashSet|LinkedList)

practices.title: Using deprecated unsafe thread-control methods (Thread.stop(), suspend(), resume())
practices.description: Thread.stop() can terminate a thread at any arbitrary point, potentially leaving shared objects (and any locks the thread held) in a corrupted, inconsistent state
practices.risk: suspend()/resume() are deadlock-prone because a suspended thread can hold a lock that the resuming thread needs. All three have been deprecated for removal for exactly these reasons.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_ANNOTATION_HEURISTIC: Thread.stop()/Thread.suspend()/Thread.resume() called on a Thread instance

practices.title: Not attaching exceptionally()/handle() to a CompletableFuture chain
practices.description: If a stage in a CompletableFuture pipeline throws and nothing downstream calls exceptionally(), handle(), or eventually get()/join(), the failure can go completely unobserved
practices.risk: the future simply completes exceptionally and nothing in the application ever finds out.
practices.code:
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(this::riskyOperation)
    .thenApply(this::transform)
    .thenAccept(this::save); // if riskyOperation() throws, this chain fails silently — nothing logs or reacts to it
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: CompletableFuture chain ending in thenAccept()/thenRun() with no exceptionally()/handle()/whenComplete() anywhere in the chain

practices.title: Not propagating request-scoped context (MDC, security context) into asynchronously submitted tasks
practices.description: MDC values, security/authentication context, and other thread-bound state set up for the current request don't automatically transfer to a task run on a different thread via an executor or @Async
practices.risk: logs from the async task lose their correlation ID, and security checks inside it may see no authenticated principal at all.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: MDC values or security context not explicitly propagated into a task submitted to an ExecutorService or an @Async method

practices.title: Not unwrapping CompletionException/ExecutionException to get the actual root cause
practices.description: join() throws CompletionException and get() throws ExecutionException, both of which wrap the real exception thrown inside the async computation
practices.risk: logging or checking the wrapper type directly instead of its getCause() hides what actually failed.
practices.detectionPattern: catch\s*\(\s*(?:CompletionException|ExecutionException)\s+(\w+)\s*\)\s*\{(?:(?!\1\.getCause\(\))[\s\S]){0,300}\}

practices.title: Over-subscribing CPU-bound thread pools beyond the number of available cores
practices.description: For purely CPU-bound work, running more threads than available cores doesn't increase throughput
practices.risk: it adds context-switching overhead as the OS scheduler shuffles more runnable threads than it has cores to run them on, typically making things slower rather than faster.
practices.code:
ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(200); // for a CPU-bound task on an 8-core machine
// most threads spend their time context-switching rather than computing
practices.solution:
int cores = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors();
ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(cores); // sized to match CPU-bound work to actual parallelism available
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: fixed thread pool size hardcoded far above availableProcessors() for CPU-bound work

practices.title: Acquiring a Semaphore permit without releasing it in a finally block
practices.description: If code between acquire() and release() throws, and release() isn't in a finally block, the permit is never returned to the semaphore
practices.risk: over time, permits leak away until no thread can acquire one at all, effectively deadlocking the whole resource pool.

practices.title: Using ReentrantLock without unlocking in a finally block
practices.description: Unlike synchronized, which automatically releases its lock even on exception, ReentrantLock requires an explicit unlock() call
practices.risk: if that call isn't in a finally block, an exception thrown while the lock is held leaves it locked forever, blocking every other thread that needs it.

practices.title: Assuming ReentrantLock is fair by default
practices.description: ReentrantLock() with no arguments creates an unfair lock
practices.risk: can grant access to a thread that just requested it ahead of threads that have been waiting longer — this generally gives better throughput, but code that expects FIFO fairness (e.g. for a specific ordering guarantee) needs to explicitly request it.
practices.code: Lock lock = new ReentrantLock(); // unfair by default — no ordering guarantee for waiting threads
practices.solution: Lock lock = new ReentrantLock(true); // fair — grants access in roughly the order threads requested it, at some throughput cost
practices.detectionPattern: new\s+ReentrantLock\s*\(\s*\)

practices.title: Using the same thread-pool-sizing formula for both CPU-bound and I/O-bound workloads
practices.description: CPU-bound work benefits from a pool sized near the core count (more threads just add contention), while I/O-bound work
practices.risk: where threads spend most of their time blocked waiting on network/disk — benefits from a much larger pool, since blocked threads aren't consuming CPU. Applying one flat rule to both wastes capacity in one case and starves it in the other.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: identical thread-pool-size constant applied to executors with very different CPU-vs-I/O-wait task profiles

practices.title: Pooling virtual threads instead of creating a new one per task
practices.description: Virtual threads are intentionally cheap to create (thousands can exist at once with minimal overhead)
practices.risk: the traditional motivation for pooling — avoiding the cost of thread creation — doesn't apply; wrapping them in a fixed-size pool reintroduces the very throughput ceiling (limited concurrent threads) that virtual threads exist to remove.
practices.code: ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(200, Thread.ofVirtual().factory()); // artificially caps concurrency at 200, defeating the purpose
practices.solution: ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); // creates one new virtual thread per submitted task, no pooling/capping
practices.detectionPattern: Executors\.newFixedThreadPool\([^,]+,\s*Thread\.ofVirtual\(\)\.factory\(\)\)

practices.title: Waiting on multiple futures sequentially instead of fanning out with CompletableFuture.allOf()
practices.description: Calling .get() on each future one at a time, right after submitting it, effectively serializes work that could have run concurrently
practices.risk: the total wait time becomes the sum of all task durations instead of roughly the duration of the slowest one.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: multiple independent executor.submit(...).get() calls made one after another rather than submitted first and joined together

practices.title: Using Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor() but expecting parallel execution
practices.description: A single-thread executor processes submitted tasks strictly one at a time, in submission order
practices.risk: code that submits several tasks expecting them to run concurrently (to speed things up) gets no parallelism at all and may be surprised when total time equals the sum of all task durations.
practices.detectionPattern: Executors\.newSingleThreadExecutor\(\)

practices.title: Assuming a custom lock implementation is reentrant when it isn't
practices.description: Java's intrinsic (synchronized) locks and ReentrantLock both allow the thread already holding a lock to acquire it again without blocking
practices.risk: a hand-rolled lock (e.g. built directly on a Semaphore with 1 permit) typically does not have this property, so a thread that locks and then, directly or via a nested call, tries to lock again deadlocks against itself.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: a custom or Semaphore-based mutual-exclusion mechanism whose acquire path can be re-entered by the same thread

practices.title: Synchronizing on interned String literals as lock objects
practices.description: String literals are interned and shared JVM-wide (and across libraries)
practices.risk: synchronized("some-key") locks on the exact same object as any other unrelated code in the entire application that happens to use the identical literal — creating invisible cross-module contention or even deadlock between completely unrelated features.
practices.detectionPattern: synchronized\s*\(\s*\"[^\"]*\"\s*\)

practices.title: Using cached autoboxed values (Boolean, small Integer) as lock objects
practices.description: Boolean.TRUE/Boolean.FALSE and small Integer values (-128 to 127, via autoboxing) are cached singletons shared throughout the JVM
practices.risk: synchronizing on one of these shared instances has the same unintended cross-code contention risk as locking on an interned String literal.
practices.detectionPattern: synchronized\s*\(\s*Boolean\.(?:TRUE|FALSE)\s*\)

practices.title: Writer starvation from constant reader traffic on a ReadWriteLock
practices.description: ReentrantReadWriteLock's default (non-fair) policy can let a continuous stream of readers keep acquiring the read lock ahead of a waiting writer indefinitely, since readers don't block each other
practices.risk: under high read concurrency, a writer may wait far longer than expected, or in pathological cases, effectively forever.
practices.code:
ReadWriteLock rwLock = new ReentrantReadWriteLock(); // default, non-fair
// Under sustained heavy read load, a writer's lock.writeLock().lock() can be starved indefinitely
practices.solution:
ReadWriteLock rwLock = new ReentrantReadWriteLock(true); // fair mode reduces (though doesn't eliminate) writer starvation risk
// Or reconsider whether a StampedLock (optimistic reads) or a different concurrency structure fits the read/write ratio better
practices.detectionPattern: new\s+ReentrantReadWriteLock\s*\(\s*\)

practices.title: Not handling BrokenBarrierException on CyclicBarrier.await()
practices.description: If one party times out, is interrupted, or the barrier is explicitly reset while others are waiting, CyclicBarrier.await() throws BrokenBarrierException for all the remaining waiting threads
practices.risk: failing to catch it leaves those threads' exceptional paths unhandled and callers unaware the coordinated rendezvous never completed.
practices.code: barrier.await(); // if another party breaks the barrier, this throws BrokenBarrierException with no handling here

practices.title: Calling Thread.interrupt() on a thread with no interruption-aware blocking call inside it
practices.description: interrupt() only has an observable effect if the target thread is blocked in an interruptible operation (wait(), sleep(), a blocking I/O or lock call) or explicitly checks Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() in its loop
practices.risk: calling it on a thread doing tight CPU-bound work with neither is effectively a no-op — the thread never notices and never stops.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: long-running loop in manually created Thread/Runnable code with no isInterrupted() check and no interruptible blocking call

practices.title: Creating non-daemon background threads that prevent JVM shutdown
practices.description: A plain new Thread() is non-daemon by default
practices.risk: if a background/cleanup thread is meant to run only while the application is alive, forgetting to mark it as a daemon thread means the JVM won't exit until that thread finishes on its own, even after all real application work is done.
practices.detectionPattern: new\s+Thread\([^)]*\)(?![\s\S]{0,150}?setDaemon\(true\))

practices.title: Using the non-async variant (thenApply) for blocking work
practices.description: thenApply() (unlike thenApplyAsync()) runs its callback on whichever thread happens to complete the previous stage
practices.risk: which, if that stage was already complete or completed on a caller thread, could be the calling thread itself, or the limited common ForkJoinPool. Doing blocking work there can unexpectedly stall the very thread you didn't mean to block.
practices.code:
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(this::fetchData)
    .thenApply(data -> callSlowBlockingApi(data)); // may run on the common ForkJoinPool, blocking a shared resource
practices.solution:
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(this::fetchData)
    .thenApplyAsync(data -> callSlowBlockingApi(data), dedicatedExecutor); // explicit executor, isolated from shared pools
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: thenApply()/thenAccept()/thenRun() (non-Async form) whose lambda performs blocking I/O

practices.title: Protecting the same shared state with two different, inconsistent locking mechanisms
practices.description: If one code path guards a piece of shared state with a synchronized block and another path guards the same state with a separate ReentrantLock (or a different lock object entirely), the two mechanisms never exclude each other
practices.risk: both can run concurrently against the same data, giving no real mutual exclusion despite each path 'having a lock'.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: a single shared mutable field accessed under more than one distinct lock object/mechanism

practices.title: Not naming manually created threads or setting an uncaught exception handler
practices.description: A thread created without an explicit name shows up in thread dumps and profilers as a generic 'Thread-12'
practices.risk: it hard to identify during an incident; without an UncaughtExceptionHandler, an unhandled exception in that thread just prints to stderr (or is lost, depending on the environment) with nothing else in the application ever finding out it died.
practices.code: new Thread(this::backgroundTask).start(); // shows as "Thread-7" in a thread dump; if it throws, nothing else in the app notices
practices.detectionPattern: new\s+Thread\(\s*[^,()]+\)\s*(?:;|\.start)

practices.title: Running blocking calls on a reactive event-loop thread
practices.description: Reactive frameworks (e.g. WebFlux/Netty) run many concurrent requests on a small, fixed pool of event-loop threads, relying on non-blocking I/O throughout
practices.risk: a single blocking call (a synchronous JDBC query, Thread.sleep(), a blocking HTTP client) on one of these threads stalls that thread entirely, backing up every other request scheduled onto it.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: blocking I/O call (JDBC, synchronous HTTP client, Thread.sleep) invoked directly inside a Mono/Flux pipeline with no subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic())

practices.title: Not handling RejectedExecutionException when submitting to a saturated bounded ThreadPoolExecutor
practices.description: A bounded ThreadPoolExecutor with a bounded queue throws RejectedExecutionException (under the default AbortPolicy) once both the pool and its queue are full
practices.risk: code that submits tasks without catching this treats an expected backpressure signal as an unhandled crash.
practices.code: executor.submit(task); // throws RejectedExecutionException under load with no handling — propagates as an unexpected failure
practices.detectionPattern: \.(?:submit|execute)\([\s\S]{0,80}?\)\s*;(?![\s\S]{0,150}?RejectedExecutionException)

practices.title: Using an unbounded work queue in a ThreadPoolExecutor
practices.description: Executors.newFixedThreadPool() uses an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue internally
practices.risk: if tasks arrive faster than they can be processed, the queue grows without limit, consuming memory until the JVM runs out — there's no backpressure signal, just a slow-motion OutOfMemoryError under sustained overload.
practices.code: ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10); // unbounded queue underneath — no limit on how many tasks can pile up
practices.detectionPattern: Executors\.newFixedThreadPool\(

practices.title: Ignoring the boolean return value of compareAndSet()
practices.description: compareAndSet() only updates the value if it currently equals the expected value, returning false and doing nothing otherwise
practices.risk: code that calls it and assumes the update always happened (without checking the return value or retrying in a loop) silently proceeds with stale state after a failed CAS.
practices.code:
atomicRef.compareAndSet(oldValue, newValue); // return value discarded — if another thread changed it first, this silently did nothing
useNewValue(); // assumes the update succeeded, but it may not have
practices.detectionPattern: (?<!if\s\()\w+\.compareAndSet\([^()]*\)\s*;

practices.title: Keeping a reference to the original unwrapped collection after wrapping it for synchronization
practices.description: Collections.synchronizedList(list) returns a new wrapper object
practices.risk: the thread-safety guarantee only applies to calls made through that wrapper. If code elsewhere still holds and uses the original 'list' reference directly, those accesses bypass synchronization entirely, defeating the whole point of wrapping it.
practices.solution:
List<String> safeList = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>()); // no separate reference to the raw list ever escapes
safeList.add("x"); // always goes through the synchronized wrapper
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: a variable holding the pre-wrapped collection that remains reachable/used after Collections.synchronizedXxx() has been called on it

practices.title: Circular static initialization between two classes causing a class-loading deadlock
practices.description: If class A's static initializer (or a static field initializer) triggers loading of class B, and class B's static initializer triggers loading of class A, two threads loading A and B concurrently (one starting with A, the other with B) can each block waiting for the other's class-initialization lock, deadlocking the whole application at startup.
practices.risk: Two threads loading A and B concurrently can each block waiting for the other's class-initialization lock, deadlocking the whole application at startup with no obvious stack trace pointing at the real cause.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: two classes whose static initializers reference each other, directly or transitively

practices.title: Not closing a StructuredTaskScope in a try-with-resources block
practices.description: StructuredTaskScope (Java 21+ preview) ties the lifetime of all subtasks it forks to the scope itself
practices.risk: failing to use try-with-resources (or forgetting to call close()) means subtasks aren't guaranteed to be joined or cancelled together, undermining the entire point of structuring their concurrency.
practices.detectionPattern: (?<!try \()(?<!try \(var )new\s+StructuredTaskScope\.

practices.title: Coupling business logic to Thread.currentThread().getName() or thread identity
practices.description: Making a decision (which branch to take
practices.risk: resource to use) based on the current thread's name or identity ties correctness to incidental scheduling/threading details that can change with any refactor of the executor, thread pool, or framework version — it's fragile and nearly impossible to reason about or test reliably.
practices.detectionPattern: Thread\.currentThread\(\)\.getName\(\)

practices.title: Chaining blocking get()/join() calls inside an async CompletableFuture stage
practices.description: Calling get()/join() on another future from inside a thenApply()/thenCompose() callback blocks whichever thread is executing that stage, defeating the purpose of composing futures asynchronously
practices.risk: thenCompose() exists specifically to chain dependent async operations without ever blocking a thread.
practices.solution: future1.thenCompose(result -> future2); // chains the two futures without blocking any thread; the pipeline completes when future2 does

practices.title: Ignoring false sharing when hot fields used by different threads share a CPU cache line
practices.description: When two independently-updated fields (e.g. per-thread counters in an array of adjacent longs) happen to sit on the same CPU cache line, writes by one thread invalidate the cache line for all cores, forcing expensive cache-coherency traffic even though the threads never touch each other's actual data
practices.risk: a purely mechanical-sympathy performance issue, not a correctness one.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: independently-updated fields declared adjacently in a hot, highly-concurrent class; best identified via profiling, not static review

practices.title: Shipping high-throughput services with default thread pool and queue sizes, never load-tested
practices.description: Framework and library defaults for thread pool sizes, queue capacities, and connection pool limits are generic starting points, not tuned for any particular service's actual traffic shape
practices.risk: deploying without load-testing under realistic concurrency means the first time real limits get discovered is during a production incident.
practices.code:
// Server started with every executor, connection pool, and queue left at its library default,
// with no load test ever run above a handful of manual requests before going live.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: executor/connection-pool/queue configuration left at framework defaults for a service with meaningful production traffic and no load-test evidence

practices.title: String concatenation in a loop
practices.description: Each += on a String allocates a new String; over N iterations this is O(n^2). StringBuilder amortizes to O(n).
practices.risk: Fine in a unit test with 5 rows, then times out or spikes latency once a real dataset with thousands of rows hits it.

practices.title: Creating unnecessary objects in a hot path
practices.description: Effective Java Item 6: creating an equivalent object repeatedly (a fresh regex Pattern, a new wrapper) when an immutable/reusable one would do wastes allocation and GC pressure for no benefit.
practices.risk: A method compiling the same regex on every call, or called in a loop over thousands of rows, spends measurable CPU time on object creation instead of the actual work.

practices.title: Using exceptions for ordinary control flow
practices.description: Effective Java Item 69: exceptions are for exceptional conditions. Using them to control a normal loop is slower than a plain condition check and obscures intent.
practices.risk: Throwing and catching an exception on every iteration of a hot loop costs orders of magnitude more than a bounds check, and confuses readers about whether the 'exceptional' path is actually expected.
practices.detectionPattern: catch\s*\(\s*ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException

practices.title: Busy-waiting with Thread.sleep() instead of proper synchronization
practices.description: Polling a condition in a sleep loop wastes CPU and reacts late (up to one sleep interval late) instead of responding the instant the condition becomes true.
practices.risk: Under load, many busy-waiting threads burn CPU that real work needs, and the artificial polling delay adds latency that a wait/notify or CompletableFuture wouldn't have.
practices.solution:
task.thenAccept(this::processResult);
// or: CountDownLatch / Object.wait()-notify() for the blocking case
practices.detectionPattern: while\s*\([^)]*\)\s*\{\s*Thread\.sleep

practices.title: Using Vector/Hashtable/StringBuffer in single-threaded code
practices.description: These legacy classes synchronize every method call. In code that's never accessed from multiple threads, that's pure overhead with no benefit — ArrayList/HashMap/StringBuilder do the same job faster.
practices.risk: Every single-threaded call pays a lock acquisition/release cost for no reason; under profiling this shows up as unexplained synchronization overhead in a supposedly single-threaded path.
practices.code:
Vector<Order> orders = new Vector<>();
StringBuffer sb = new StringBuffer();
practices.solution:
List<Order> orders = new ArrayList<>();
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
practices.detectionPattern: \bnew\s+(Vector|Hashtable|StringBuffer)\b

practices.title: Overusing parallelStream() without understanding overhead or thread-safety
practices.description: parallelStream() shares a common fork-join pool across the whole application.
practices.risk: For small collections or I/O-bound/non-thread-safe operations it can be slower than sequential and introduces race conditions on shared mutable state.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: parallelStream() on small collections, on I/O-bound operations, or pipelines that mutate shared non-thread-safe state.

practices.title: Using Stream<Integer>/Stream<Long> instead of IntStream/LongStream/DoubleStream for numeric work
practices.description: Stream<Integer> boxes every element, causing unnecessary object allocation and unboxing overhead during numeric aggregation compared to the dedicated primitive stream types.
practices.risk: A hot numeric aggregation path pays for boxing every element instead of running as fast, allocation-free primitive arithmetic.
practices.code:
Stream<Integer> nums = list.stream().map(Item::getQuantity);
int total = nums.reduce(0, Integer::sum); // boxes every element
practices.solution:
int total = list.stream()
    .mapToInt(Item::getQuantity)
    .sum(); // IntStream avoids boxing entirely
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Stream<Integer>/Stream<Long>/Stream<Double> pipelines used purely for sum/average/min/max instead of mapToInt/mapToLong/mapToDouble.

practices.title: Not setting initial capacity for collections with a known size
practices.description: Default collection capacities force repeated internal resizing and array copying as elements are added.
practices.risk: When the final size is known or estimable in advance, this is wasted work.
practices.code:
List<String> results = new ArrayList<>(); // default capacity 10
for (Row row : hugeResultSet) { // e.g. 100,000 rows
    results.add(row.toString()); // repeated resizes/copies as it grows
}
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: new ArrayList<>()/new HashMap<>() with no capacity argument, immediately followed by a loop with a known or easily obtainable bound.

practices.title: Using nested loops for lookups instead of building a Map for O(1) access
practices.description: Searching one list inside a loop over another produces O(n*m) complexity.
practices.risk: Indexing the smaller collection into a Map up front turns repeated lookups into O(1) each.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Nested loops where the inner loop searches for a matching element by field comparison instead of using a pre-built Map/Set.

practices.title: Using HashMap<EnumType, V> instead of EnumMap for enum-keyed maps
practices.description: EnumMap is implemented as a compact array indexed by enum ordinal, giving better performance and predictable (natural enum) iteration order compared to a general-purpose HashMap keyed by enum constants.
practices.risk: A map keyed by a small enum runs slower and iterates in an arbitrary order instead of the enum's natural declaration order, for no benefit over EnumMap.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: HashMap/TreeMap declared with an enum type as the key type parameter.

practices.title: Using findFirst() on a parallel stream when order doesn't matter
practices.description: findFirst() must respect encounter order even on a parallel stream, which forces extra coordination overhead.
practices.risk: When any matching element is acceptable, findAny() lets the runtime return as soon as one is found, which is faster in parallel.
practices.code:
Optional<Order> match = orders.parallelStream()
    .filter(o -> o.getStatus() == Status.URGENT)
    .findFirst(); // forces ordered coordination even though caller doesn't care which URGENT order it gets
practices.solution:
Optional<Order> match = orders.parallelStream()
    .filter(o -> o.getStatus() == Status.URGENT)
    .findAny(); // no ordering constraint, faster in parallel
// Use findFirst() only when a deterministic, encounter-order result is actually required
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: findFirst() used after parallelStream() where the surrounding code doesn't depend on which specific match is returned.

practices.title: Filtering a stream twice instead of using Collectors.partitioningBy()
practices.description: Splitting a collection into two groups by a boolean predicate is commonly done with two separate filter() passes over the same source, which traverses the data twice when a single partitioningBy() collector does it in one pass.
practices.risk: The source collection is traversed twice to build two lists that a single partitioningBy() pass would produce from one traversal.
practices.code:
List<Order> paid = orders.stream().filter(Order::isPaid).collect(Collectors.toList());
List<Order> unpaid = orders.stream().filter(o -> !o.isPaid()).collect(Collectors.toList()); // two full traversals
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Two filter()...collect() pipelines over the same source collection where the predicates are logical negations of each other.

practices.title: Recomputing Collections.max()/min() or sorting inside a loop instead of precomputing once
practices.description: Calling max()/min()/sort() on the same (or growing) collection repeatedly inside a loop is O(n) or O(n log n) per iteration, turning an otherwise linear algorithm into quadratic or worse.
practices.risk: An O(n) or O(n log n) computation that could run once instead re-runs on every loop iteration, turning a linear algorithm quadratic or worse.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Collections.max()/min()/sort() or stream().sorted()/max()/min() called inside a loop body where the underlying collection doesn't change between iterations.

practices.title: Not reordering stream operations for efficiency (sorting/mapping before filtering)
practices.description: Placing an expensive operation like sorted() or a costly map() before filter() forces it to run on every element, even ones that will be discarded.
practices.risk: Filtering first reduces the working set before the expensive step runs.
practices.code:
list.stream()
    .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Item::getExpensiveKey)) // sorts everything first
    .filter(Item::isActive) // then throws most of it away
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
practices.solution:
list.stream()
    .filter(Item::isActive) // shrink the working set first
    .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Item::getExpensiveKey)) // sort only what remains
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Stream pipelines where sorted()/map() with an expensive function precedes a filter() that would have reduced the element count.

practices.title: Making two separate stream passes to compute two aggregates instead of Collectors.teeing()
practices.description: Computing two different aggregates (e.g. sum and count, or min and max) by streaming the source collection twice does double the traversal work.
practices.risk: Collectors.teeing() (Java 12+) computes both in a single pass and merges the results.
practices.code:
double total = orders.stream().mapToDouble(Order::getAmount).sum(); // pass 1
long count = orders.stream().count(); // pass 2 — same source traversed again
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Two or more independent terminal operations invoked on separately-created streams from the same source collection within the same method.

practices.title: Using HashSet<EnumType> instead of EnumSet for enum-based sets
practices.description: EnumSet is a bit-vector implementation specialized for enum types, giving much better performance and memory usage than a general-purpose HashSet, plus iteration in natural (declaration) order.
practices.risk: A small, fixed enum-backed set pays general-purpose HashSet overhead instead of EnumSet's compact bit-vector representation, with no corresponding benefit.
practices.solution: Set<DayOfWeek> weekend = EnumSet.of(DayOfWeek.SATURDAY, DayOfWeek.SUNDAY); // compact, fast, ordered
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: HashSet/TreeSet declared with an enum type parameter instead of EnumSet.

practices.title: Creating excessive short-lived objects inside hot loops
practices.description: Allocating new objects (formatters, small helper objects, boxed values, temporary arrays) on every iteration of a hot loop increases young-generation garbage collection frequency
practices.risk: hoisting reusable, stateless objects outside the loop cuts allocation rate and GC pause frequency significantly.
practices.detectionPattern: for\s*\([^)]*\)\s*\{(?:(?!\}).)*?new\s+SimpleDateFormat\(

practices.title: Running a memory- or latency-sensitive service entirely on default JVM heap/GC settings
practices.description: Default heap sizing (a fraction of available system memory) and the default garbage collector are general-purpose choices, not tuned for any specific service's allocation rate, object lifetimes, or latency requirements
practices.risk: a service under real production load with no tuning or observability into GC behavior can hit unpredictable pauses or OutOfMemoryErrors that would have been visible and preventable with basic GC logging and heap sizing.
practices.code:
# Deployed with no -Xmx, -Xms, or GC-related flags at all, and no GC logging enabled
java -jar service.jar
practices.solution:
java -Xms2g -Xmx2g -XX:+UseG1GC -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime:filecount=5,filesize=50M -jar service.jar
# Explicit heap sizing avoids surprise resizing, GC logging gives visibility for tuning based on real production behavior
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: production deployment configuration with no explicit -Xmx/-Xms or GC-related JVM flags for a service handling meaningful load

practices.title: Never evaluating GC algorithm choice for workloads with strict pause-time requirements
practices.description: Different garbage collectors trade off throughput, memory overhead, and pause time differently (G1 balances both, ZGC/Shenandoah target near-zero pause times at some throughput/memory cost)
practices.risk: a latency-sensitive service (e.g. trading, real-time bidding) left on whichever GC happens to be the JVM's default may suffer pause-time spikes that a purpose-evaluated collector would largely avoid.
practices.code:
# Latency-critical service deployed with whatever the JVM's default GC happens to be, never benchmarked against alternatives
java -jar latency-critical-service.jar
practices.solution:
# After benchmarking G1 vs ZGC against this service's actual allocation pattern and latency SLOs:
java -XX:+UseZGC -Xmx8g -jar latency-critical-service.jar
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: latency-sensitive service left on default GC algorithm with no benchmarking evidence or explicit GC selection rationale

practices.title: Repeatedly performing reflective lookups in hot paths instead of caching the result
practices.description: Class.getMethod()/getField()/getDeclaredConstructor() perform a linear search and security checks internally
practices.risk: calling them fresh on every invocation of a hot method, rather than resolving once and caching the resulting Method/Field/Constructor object, adds significant avoidable overhead to a path that may run millions of times.
practices.detectionPattern: \.get(?:Declared)?(?:Method|Constructor)\(\s*\"|\.getDeclaredField\(\s*\"

practices.title: Implementing manual object pools for cheap, short-lived objects
practices.description: Modern generational garbage collectors are specifically optimized for allocating and quickly reclaiming many small, short-lived objects
practices.risk: often faster than the synchronization and bookkeeping overhead a hand-rolled object pool introduces; pooling is really only worth it for genuinely expensive-to-create objects (large buffers, DB connections, threads), not everyday POJOs.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: hand-written object pool (acquire()/release() pattern) wrapping small, cheap-to-construct value objects

practices.title: Optimizing performance based on guesswork instead of profiling data
practices.description: Intuition about where an application spends its time is frequently wrong
practices.risk: rewriting a piece of code to be 'faster' without measuring first can add complexity and risk for a code path that was never actually a bottleneck, while the real hotspot goes unaddressed.
practices.code:
// "This loop looks slow, let's rewrite it with manual array indexing and micro-optimize the arithmetic"
// ...spends a day on a method that profiling would have shown accounts for 0.1% of total request time
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: performance-motivated code change with no accompanying profiling data, benchmark numbers, or before/after measurements

practices.title: Not presizing StringBuilder for a known large output
practices.description: StringBuilder's default initial capacity (16 characters) forces repeated internal char-array resizing and copying as content is appended
practices.risk: when the final size is roughly known in advance, passing it to the constructor avoids most or all of that resizing overhead.
practices.detectionPattern: new\s+StringBuilder\(\s*\)

practices.title: Rebuilding a fresh defensive copy of large immutable data on every call instead of caching it once
practices.description: If the underlying data genuinely never changes, returning a brand-new defensive copy (a cloned array, a freshly-collected list) from a getter on every single call repeats the same allocation and copy work unnecessarily
practices.risk: computing the immutable copy once and caching it avoids the repeated cost entirely.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: getter that reloads/recomputes/re-copies a value from a static or rarely-changing source on every invocation

practices.title: Using ArrayList as a queue via repeated remove(0)
practices.description: ArrayList.remove(0) is O(n) because every remaining element must shift down by one position
practices.risk: using this pattern in a loop to drain a list FIFO-style turns what should be a linear-time operation into a quadratic one as the list shrinks.
practices.detectionPattern: \.remove\(\s*0\s*\)

practices.title: Repeatedly reloading configuration or resource files at runtime instead of caching them at startup
practices.description: Reading and parsing a configuration file, properties file, or static resource from disk/classpath on every request (rather than once at startup or on genuine change) adds unnecessary I/O and parsing overhead to every call, when the content rarely or never changes during the application's lifetime.
practices.risk: Every request pays avoidable I/O and parsing latency for content that never changes during the application's lifetime.
practices.detectionPattern: new\s+Properties\(\)\s*;[\s\S]{0,100}?\.load\(

practices.title: Unnecessary heap allocations that defeat JIT escape analysis
practices.description: The JIT compiler can sometimes allocate small, non-escaping objects on the stack (or eliminate them entirely) instead of the heap, avoiding GC overhead altogether
practices.risk: but only if the object's lifetime and references are simple enough for the compiler to prove it never 'escapes' the method. Passing such objects through extra layers of indirection (storing them in fields, passing them to non-inlined methods) can defeat this optimization, forcing a real heap allocation that otherwise wouldn't have been needed.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: small, purely local helper objects passed into non-trivial method calls in extremely hot, allocation-sensitive code; best confirmed via JIT/escape-analysis profiling

practices.title: Calling System.gc() in application code, assuming it forces an immediate full collection
practices.description: System.gc() is only a hint that suggests the JVM run garbage collection soon
practices.risk: the JVM is free to ignore it entirely, and on some collectors, honoring it triggers an expensive full-heap collection at exactly the wrong moment (e.g. mid-request), causing a latency spike the application inflicted on itself.
