# In-flight requests get up to 30s to complete before the server actually stops accepting new work and shuts down
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: application configuration with no server.shutdown: graceful setting for a service deployed behind a load balancer

practices.title: Giving a default value to a @Value property that should actually be mandatory
practices.description: Adding a fallback default (@Value("${some.required.prop:fallback}")) to a property that the application genuinely cannot function correctly without turns a missing-configuration error (which would surface immediately and clearly at startup) into silent misconfiguration that only manifests as wrong behavior much later.
practices.risk: A genuinely missing production configuration value silently falls back to a dev-only default instead of failing fast at startup with a clear error.
practices.code:
@Value("${payment.gateway.url:http://localhost:8080}") // masks a genuinely missing production config with a dev-only fallback
private String gatewayUrl;
practices.detectionPattern: @Value\(\s*\"\$\{[^:}]+:(?:localhost|changeme|CHANGEME)[^}]*\}\"\s*\)

practices.title: Not enabling fail-fast configuration validation for required properties
practices.description: Without explicit validation (via @ConfigurationProperties + @Validated, or a startup-time check), missing or malformed required configuration doesn't produce a clear, actionable startup error
practices.risk: it either falls back to a default silently or fails later with a confusing NullPointerException deep in unrelated business logic, far from the actual root cause.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: required configuration properties read via unvalidated @Value fields rather than centralized, validated @ConfigurationProperties classes

practices.title: Assuming ContextRefreshedEvent fires exactly once
practices.description: ContextRefreshedEvent fires every time the application context is refreshed
practices.risk: which happens once at normal startup, but also again in scenarios like Spring Boot DevTools' automatic restart or certain testing setups that refresh the context multiple times; a listener with one-time-only initialization logic and no idempotency guard runs that logic again on each refresh.
practices.detectionPattern: @EventListener\(\s*ContextRefreshedEvent\.class\s*\)

practices.title: Not using @Order on multiple BeanPostProcessor/ApplicationListener beans with interdependent execution requirements
practices.description: When several BeanPostProcessor or ApplicationListener implementations need to run in a specific relative order (one preparing state the next one depends on), leaving their execution order to Spring's default (registration order
practices.risk: itself depends on component-scan order) makes the correctness of the whole chain accidental rather than guaranteed.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: multiple BeanPostProcessor/ApplicationListener implementations with an implicit dependency on relative execution order and no @Order/Ordered

practices.title: Placing proxy-based annotations on a final class or final method
practices.description: Spring's CGLIB-based proxying (used for class-based proxies, e.g. classes without interfaces) works by generating a subclass that overrides the target's methods
practices.risk: it cannot override final methods and cannot subclass a final class at all, so @Transactional/@Async/@Cacheable on a final class or method is silently ignored — no error, the annotation just has no effect.
practices.detectionPattern: (?:final\s+class\s+\w+[\s\S]{0,20}\{[\s\S]{0,300}?@(?:Transactional|Async|Cacheable))|(?:@(?:Transactional|Async|Cacheable)\s*\n\s*(?:public\s+)?final\s+[\w<>\[\]]+\s+\w+\()

practices.title: Incomplete or missing custom health indicators for critical dependencies
practices.description: Spring Boot Actuator's default health endpoint reports 'UP' based on whatever HealthIndicators are registered
practices.risk: if a critical external dependency (a payment gateway, a message broker, a specific downstream API) has no corresponding health indicator, the application can report perfectly healthy to orchestration/load-balancer health checks while that dependency is completely down, keeping unhealthy instances in rotation.
practices.code:
// Application depends critically on a payment gateway and a message broker, but only the
// default DataSource health indicator is registered — health checks pass even when payments are completely broken
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: critical external dependency (payment gateway, message broker, key downstream API) with no corresponding custom HealthIndicator bean

practices.title: Registering a custom PropertySource with lower precedence than expected
practices.description: Spring resolves properties by checking registered PropertySources in a defined precedence order
practices.risk: adding a custom PropertySource without understanding where it lands in that order can mean its values are silently overridden by another source (environment variables, command-line args, application.yml) with no visible error — the property 'exists' but a different value always wins.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: custom PropertySource registration where a property's resolved value doesn't match what's expected from that source

practices.title: Branching on manually-read environment variables instead of using Spring Profiles
practices.description: Reading System.getenv()/System.getProperty() directly to decide environment-specific behavior duplicates functionality Spring already provides via @Profile and profile-specific application-{profile}.yml files, and scatters environment logic through the codebase instead of centralizing it in configuration.
practices.risk: Environment logic gets scattered through the codebase instead of centralized in configuration, making it easy to miss a spot when a new environment is added.
practices.detectionPattern: System\.getenv\(\s*\"[^\"]*\"\s*\)\s*\)?\s*\.equals\(|\.equals\(\s*System\.getenv\(

practices.title: Placing business logic inside @Bean factory methods
practices.description: A @Configuration class's @Bean methods are meant to describe how to construct and wire objects
practices.risk: embedding actual business logic (data transformation, conditional branching based on business rules) there mixes two very different concerns in one place, making both the wiring and the logic harder to test and reason about independently.

practices.title: Not setting a distinct thread name prefix on custom @Async/@Scheduled executors
practices.description: A custom TaskExecutor left with its default thread naming produces generic names (e.g. 'pool-1-thread-3') indistinguishable from any other pool in a thread dump
practices.risk: it much harder to tell which threads belong to which subsystem when diagnosing a production issue.
practices.detectionPattern: new\s+ThreadPoolTaskExecutor\(\)(?![\s\S]{0,300}?setThreadNamePrefix\()

practices.title: Hand-rolling ad-hoc retry loops instead of using Spring Retry
practices.description: Manually writing retry loops with while/for and Thread.sleep() around fallible calls, differently in every service, produces inconsistent backoff strategies, retry limits, and exception filtering across the codebase
practices.risk: Spring Retry's @Retryable centralizes this into a declarative, consistently-configured, well-tested mechanism.

practices.title: Embedding complex SpEL expressions inside @Value strings
practices.description: Spring Expression Language inside @Value("#{...}") is powerful
practices.risk: complex logic expressed as a string embedded in an annotation is much harder to read, unit test, statically analyze, or debug than the equivalent plain Java code in a method or a properly-typed @ConfigurationProperties class.
practices.code:
@Value("#{${feature.thresholds} != null and ${feature.thresholds}.contains('premium') ? 100 : 10}")
private int threshold; // real conditional logic buried inside a string, invisible to normal Java tooling

practices.title: Hand-parsing a comma-separated @Value string instead of binding directly to a List
practices.description: Spring's relaxed configuration binding natively supports binding a comma-separated property value directly to a List<String>/String[]
practices.risk: manually splitting a raw string with String.split(",") reimplements functionality the framework already provides, and misses edge cases (trimming, empty entries) that the built-in binder already handles correctly.
practices.solution:
@Value("${allowed.origins}")
private List<String> allowedOrigins; // Spring's relaxed binding parses the comma-separated value directly, correctly
practices.detectionPattern: @Value\([^)]*\)\s*\n\s*private\s+String\s+\w+;[\s\S]{0,200}?\.split\(\s*\",\"\s*\)

practices.title: Duplicating complex @ConditionalOnExpression SpEL logic across multiple beans
practices.description: Copy-pasting the same non-trivial SpEL conditional expression onto several @Bean/@Component definitions means any change to that condition's logic has to be found and updated in every copy
practices.risk: a custom @Conditional implementation centralizes the logic once, reusable everywhere, and is far easier to unit test in isolation.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: the same or near-identical @ConditionalOnExpression SpEL string duplicated across two or more bean definitions

practices.title: Bypassing Spring's proper extension points with reflection-based hacks
practices.description: Spring provides well-defined extension points (BeanPostProcessor, BeanFactoryPostProcessor, ApplicationListener) specifically for intercepting or modifying bean creation and configuration
practices.risk: reaching for reflection to forcibly alter a bean's private fields or a container's internal state after the fact is fragile, breaks on framework version upgrades, and fights against the container instead of working with it.
practices.detectionPattern: setAccessible\(\s*true\s*\)[\s\S]{0,150}?\.(?:set|invoke)\(

practices.title: Using Spring Profiles as a substitute for per-request/per-user feature flags
practices.description: Profiles are resolved once at application startup and apply to the entire running instance
practices.risk: they're the right tool for per-environment configuration (dev/staging/prod), but the wrong tool for toggling behavior per individual user or request, since that would require restarting the whole application (or running separate instances per flag combination) just to change behavior for a subset of traffic.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: @Profile used to represent a user segment or feature toggle intended to vary per-request/per-user rather than a per-environment distinction

practices.title: Not documenting which profiles an application supports
practices.description: If the set of valid/expected @Profile values (dev, staging, prod, or feature-specific ones) exists only as tribal knowledge scattered across the code, anyone deploying or configuring the application has to grep the codebase to figure out what profile to activate, and a typo'd profile name (e.g. 'produciton') silently activates none of the intended beans with no warning.
practices.risk: A typo'd profile name activates none of the intended beans with no warning, and anyone deploying has to grep the codebase to even know what profile to activate.
practices.code:
// Profiles 'dev', 'staging', 'prod', and 'kafka-enabled' are used throughout the codebase,
// with no central list, README section, or startup-time validation of the activated profile name.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: no README/onboarding documentation listing the application's supported Spring profiles and their purpose

practices.title: Using field/constructor injection inside @Configuration classes instead of @Bean method parameters
practices.description: @Bean methods can simply declare their dependencies as method parameters
practices.risk: Spring resolves automatically; injecting dependencies into fields or a constructor of the @Configuration class itself instead adds indirection and makes it less obvious, at a glance, which @Bean methods actually need which dependencies.
practices.detectionPattern: @Configuration\s*\n\s*class\s+\w+\s*\{[\s\S]{0,300}?@Autowired\s*\n\s*private

practices.title: Mixing @ImportResource XML configuration into an otherwise fully-annotated application
practices.description: Introducing XML-based bean definitions alongside annotation-based configuration (without a clear, temporary migration reason) means anyone working on the codebase now has to check two entirely different configuration mechanisms to understand how a given bean is wired, doubling the cognitive overhead for no lasting benefit.
practices.risk: Anyone working on the codebase now has to check two entirely different configuration mechanisms to understand how a given bean is wired.
practices.detectionPattern: @ImportResource\(

practices.title: Leaving obsolete @Bean definitions and @Configuration classes in place after a feature is removed
practices.description: When a feature is removed but its supporting beans and configuration classes aren't cleaned up alongside it, the application context keeps constructing and wiring dead infrastructure (connections, executors, listeners) on every startup, adding startup time and cognitive overhead for functionality that no longer does anything useful.
practices.risk: The application context keeps constructing and wiring dead infrastructure (connections, executors, listeners) on every startup, adding startup time and cognitive overhead for functionality nobody uses anymore.
practices.solution:
// As part of removing a feature, its dedicated @Configuration class and @Bean definitions
// are deleted in the same change, verified by a passing contextLoads() test and a startup log review.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: @Configuration class or @Bean definitions whose only consumers were part of a feature since removed from the codebase

practices.title: Exposing all Spring Boot Actuator endpoints without restricting sensitive ones in production
practices.description: Endpoints like env, heapdump, beans, and configprops can reveal environment variables (potentially including secrets), full memory dumps, and the entire bean graph of the application
practices.risk: exposing all of them (management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=*) to the public internet hands an attacker a detailed map of the application's internals, and sometimes its secrets directly.
practices.code:
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: "*" # exposes env, heapdump, beans, threaddump, etc. — all publicly reachable if actuator isn't otherwise secured
practices.solution:
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info # only non-sensitive endpoints exposed publicly
  endpoint:
    health:
      show-details: when-authorized
# Sensitive endpoints (env, heapdump, beans) restricted to an internal network or behind authentication

practices.title: Never testing that the Spring dependency-injection graph actually loads
practices.description: It's possible to have thorough unit tests for business logic while never once verifying that the application context itself starts up correctly with all beans wired
practices.risk: a missing bean, a scope mismatch, or a circular dependency then surfaces for the first time during an actual deployment instead of in CI.
practices.code:
// Extensive @Mock-based unit tests for every service's business logic,
// but no test anywhere that actually loads the full (or a representative slice of the) ApplicationContext
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: test suite with no @SpringBootTest (or @ContextConfiguration) test verifying the application context itself loads

practices.title: Not using appropriate HTTP status codes for different outcomes
practices.description: Returning 200 OK for every response regardless of outcome (embedding success/failure in the response body instead) forces every client to parse the body just to know whether a call succeeded, defeats HTTP-aware tooling (caches, monitoring, load balancers) that relies on status codes, and misses the standard vocabulary REST already provides for common cases (404, 409, 422, etc.).
practices.risk: A client has to inspect the response body just to learn whether the call succeeded, and HTTP-aware tooling like caches and load balancers that key off status codes can't do their job at all.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: controller method returning ResponseEntity.ok()/200 for a validation failure, creation, or error outcome that has a more specific standard status code available

practices.title: Not versioning REST APIs
practices.description: Without any versioning strategy (URI path, header, or media-type based), a breaking change to an endpoint's request/response shape has no way to roll out gradually
practices.risk: every existing client breaks the instant the change deploys, with no path for old and new clients to coexist during a migration window.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: public REST API endpoint with no version segment in the URL path, version header, or versioned media type

practices.title: Returning inconsistent error response formats across different endpoints
practices.description: If one endpoint's error handler returns {"error": "message"}, another returns {"message": "...", "code": 123}, and a third lets Spring's default whitelabel error page through, every client integration has to special-case error parsing per endpoint instead of relying on one predictable error contract across the whole API.
practices.risk: Every client integration has to special-case error parsing per endpoint instead of relying on one predictable error contract across the whole API.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: more than one distinct JSON error response shape used across different controllers in the same API with no centralized @ControllerAdvice

practices.title: Using @RequestBody Map<String, Object> instead of typed DTOs
practices.description: Accepting an untyped Map for a request body avoids writing a DTO class
practices.risk: gives up compile-time field checking, IDE autocomplete, and the automatic OpenAPI/Swagger documentation Spring generates from typed classes — every field access becomes a string-keyed lookup with no guarantee it exists or has the expected type.
practices.detectionPattern: @RequestBody\s+Map<String,\s*Object>

practices.title: Returning raw objects instead of ResponseEntity, losing explicit control over headers and status
practices.description: Returning a plain object lets Spring pick a default status (200 for a normal return) and leaves no easy way to set custom headers, cache-control directives, or a specific status code for different outcomes within the same method
practices.risk: ResponseEntity makes all of that explicit and controllable.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: controller method returning a plain DTO/entity with .orElse(null) or similar, where ResponseEntity could express a distinct not-found/error outcome explicitly

practices.title: Missing Location header on 201 Created responses
practices.description: The HTTP spec and REST convention expect a 201 Created response to include a Location header pointing to the newly created resource's URL
practices.risk: omitting it forces clients to construct that URL themselves (often by guessing the ID field name and path structure) instead of simply following the header the server already knows.
practices.detectionPattern: ResponseEntity\.status\(\s*HttpStatus\.CREATED\s*\)\.body\(

practices.title: Not documenting API endpoints with OpenAPI/Swagger annotations
practices.description: Without OpenAPI annotations (or an equivalent generated spec), API consumers have no machine-readable contract to generate client SDKs from, no interactive documentation to explore, and no way to catch a mismatch between what the code actually does and what was verbally described, short of reading the controller source directly.
practices.risk: There's no way to catch a mismatch between what the code actually does and what was verbally described, short of reading the controller source directly.
practices.code:
@PostMapping("/orders")
public Order createOrder(@Valid @RequestBody OrderRequest req) { ... } // no @Operation/@ApiResponse annotations, no generated docs describing possible responses
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: public-facing REST controller with no springdoc-openapi/Swagger annotations and no generated OpenAPI spec

practices.title: Returning a generic, unhelpful response when JSON request parsing fails
practices.description: A malformed JSON body throws HttpMessageNotReadableException
practices.risk: without a dedicated handler produces Spring's generic 400 response giving the client no indication of what specifically was wrong with their payload (a typo in a field name, a type mismatch, truncated JSON) — just that something, somewhere, didn't parse.
practices.code:
// No @ExceptionHandler for HttpMessageNotReadableException — clients get Spring's default,
// generic 400 response with a message like "JSON parse error" and no further detail
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: no @ExceptionHandler (globally or per-controller) specifically for HttpMessageNotReadableException

practices.title: Using @PathVariable for optional or filterable criteria
practices.description: Path variables are meant to identify a specific resource (or resource hierarchy segment), not to express optional filtering criteria
practices.risk: using them for optional values forces multiple overlapping endpoint mappings (one with the segment, one without) to cover the 'not specified' case, where a single endpoint with @RequestParam would handle both naturally.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: two or more @GetMapping paths on the same resource differing only by presence/absence of a path segment representing an optional filter

practices.title: Inconsistent naming/casing conventions across REST endpoint paths and JSON fields
practices.description: Mixing camelCase and snake_case (or kebab-case and underscores) across different endpoints' paths and JSON field names forces every client integration to remember which convention applies where, with no way to guess correctly
practices.risk: a small thing that adds friction to every single API interaction across the whole surface area.
practices.code: GET /api/customerOrders/{orderId} -> { "order_id": 1, "customerName": "Alice" } // path uses camelCase, one field is snake_case, another is camelCase — no consistent rule
practices.solution: GET /api/customer-orders/{orderId} -> { "orderId": 1, "customerName": "Alice" } // kebab-case paths, camelCase JSON fields, applied uniformly across the entire API
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: a mix of casing conventions (camelCase, snake_case, kebab-case) across different endpoint paths or JSON field names in the same API

practices.title: Implementing HTTP method override via a query parameter/header instead of using the correct verb directly
practices.description: Method override (e.g. a _method=DELETE query parameter, common historically to work around HTML forms that can't send DELETE/PUT) adds an unnecessary layer of indirection for a server-to-server or modern JS-client API that can simply issue the correct HTTP verb natively
practices.risk: keeping it around without that legacy constraint just adds a second, less obvious way to trigger the same behavior.
practices.detectionPattern: @RequestParam\(\s*\"_method\"\s*\)|X-HTTP-Method-Override

practices.title: Not standardizing error handling across multiple microservices in the same system
practices.description: If each microservice in a system independently invents its own @ControllerAdvice error format, any client (or API gateway) that talks to more than one of them has to implement separate error-parsing logic per service, and cross-service tracing/correlation becomes harder since there's no shared error contract to rely on.
practices.risk: Any client or API gateway that talks to more than one service needs a separate error-parsing implementation per service, and cross-service tracing becomes harder with no shared error contract.
practices.solution:
// A shared library defines one ErrorResponse DTO and a base GlobalExceptionHandler that every
// microservice in the organization extends/reuses, ensuring one consistent error contract system-wide.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: different microservices in the same system returning different JSON error response shapes with no shared contract or common library

practices.title: Combining multiple unrelated resources into a single catch-all endpoint
practices.description: An endpoint like POST /api/execute or GET /api/data that takes an 'action' or 'type' parameter and branches internally to handle entirely unrelated operations abandons REST's resource-oriented design entirely
practices.risk: the API impossible to document, cache, authorize, or rate-limit sensibly per operation, since everything funnels through one undifferentiated URL.
practices.detectionPattern: String\s+action\s*=\s*\(String\)\s*\w+\.get\(\s*\"action\"\s*\)

practices.title: Not documenting or enforcing required vs optional query parameters
practices.description: Leaving @RequestParam's required attribute at its implicit default and never documenting whether a given query parameter is mandatory means clients discover the actual requirement by trial and error
practices.risk: a missing 'required' parameter either throws a confusing 400 with no clear message, or worse, silently falls through to unintended default behavior.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: @RequestParam with no explicit required attribute and no accompanying documentation stating whether omitting it is valid

practices.title: Inconsistent handling of 'no results' across similar endpoints
practices.description: If one list endpoint returns 200 with an empty array when nothing matches, while a similar endpoint elsewhere in the same API returns 404 for the same kind of 'nothing found' situation, clients can't apply one consistent error-handling rule across the API
practices.risk: they have to special-case each endpoint's specific convention.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: similar list-returning endpoints differing in whether an empty result returns 200 with an empty collection or a 404

practices.title: Returning different DTO shapes for the same logical resource across different endpoints
practices.description: If GET /orders/{id} returns an Order with a status field as a string enum name
practices.risk: GET /orders (the list version) returns a differently-shaped OrderSummary with status as a numeric code, clients working with 'the same' resource across two endpoints have to handle two incompatible representations of the same underlying concept, multiplying integration effort for no real benefit.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: two or more DTOs representing the same logical resource concept using different types or encodings for what should be the same field

practices.title: Not supporting HEAD requests for resource-existence checks
practices.description: HEAD is defined to return exactly the headers a GET would, with no body
practices.risk: a client that only wants to check whether a resource exists (or get its size/last-modified date) has to fetch the entire body via GET if HEAD isn't supported, wasting bandwidth and processing for information a HEAD response could have provided far more cheaply.
practices.code:
@GetMapping("/documents/{id}") // the only way to check if a document exists is downloading its entire content via GET
public ResponseEntity<byte[]> getDocument(@PathVariable Long id) { ... }
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: client need to check resource existence/metadata without downloading content, with no verification that HEAD is actually supported

practices.title: Removing or breaking old API endpoints without a deprecation period
practices.description: Deleting or changing an existing endpoint's behavior in the same release that removes the old version gives consumers zero warning and zero time to migrate
practices.risk: a deprecation period (marking the endpoint deprecated, communicating a sunset date, ideally via a Deprecation/Sunset HTTP header) lets clients migrate on their own schedule instead of breaking without notice.
practices.code:
// v1.5 release notes: "Removed /v1/orders/search (replaced by /v2/orders/search)" — with no prior deprecation
// warning in v1.4, so every client still using the old endpoint breaks the moment v1.5 deploys
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: endpoint removal or breaking behavior change in a changelog with no corresponding prior deprecation notice or Deprecation/Sunset headers

practices.title: Using @RequestParam Map<String, String> to accept arbitrary, unbounded query parameters
practices.description: Binding all query parameters into an open-ended Map gives up any control over which parameters are actually valid, how many can be supplied, or what they mean
practices.risk: a client can send hundreds of unexpected parameters, and there's no schema, validation, or documentation describing what's actually accepted.
practices.detectionPattern: @RequestParam\s+Map<String,\s*String>|@RequestParam\s+MultiValueMap<

practices.title: Inconsistent trailing-slash handling across endpoints
practices.description: Depending on configuration, /orders and /orders/ can either be treated as identical or as entirely distinct mappings
practices.risk: if this isn't handled consistently, clients get confusing 404s for a URL that looks functionally identical to one that works, with no clear rule for which form is 'correct'.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: API documentation or client-reported 404s caused by a trailing-slash mismatch with no consistent, documented policy

practices.title: Inconsistent date/time formats across different endpoints
practices.description: If one endpoint returns dates as ISO-8601 strings, another as epoch milliseconds, and a third as a custom 'MM/dd/yyyy' string, every client integration needs separate parsing logic per endpoint, and it's easy to introduce timezone or format bugs when the convention isn't uniform across the API.
practices.risk: Every client integration needs separate parsing logic per endpoint, and it's easy to introduce timezone or format bugs when the convention isn't uniform.
practices.code:
// GET /orders/{id} -> { "createdAt": "2026-09-17T10:00:00Z" } // ISO-8601
// GET /invoices/{id} -> { "createdAt": 1758100800000 } // epoch millis, same conceptual field, different encoding
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: different date/time field encodings (ISO-8601, epoch millis, custom string) used across multiple endpoints in the same API

practices.title: Not applying @JsonFormat/@DateTimeFormat consistently across DTOs
practices.description: Without explicit format annotations, date/time serialization behavior depends on Jackson's default configuration (which can itself change between library versions or global ObjectMapper customizations)
practices.risk: relying on that implicit default per-field, rather than declaring the format explicitly on each date field, risks silent format changes when shared configuration is touched for an unrelated reason.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_ANNOTATION_HEURISTIC: date/time-typed DTO field (not a JPA @Entity field, which is never directly serialized) with no @JsonFormat/@DateTimeFormat annotation

practices.title: Not including a correlation/trace ID in response headers or error bodies
practices.description: When a client reports 'my request failed', without a trace/correlation ID surfaced to them there's no efficient way to find the exact corresponding server-side log entries among potentially millions of requests
practices.risk: support and debugging end up guessing based on approximate timestamps instead of a precise, shared identifier.
practices.code:
// Error responses contain only a generic message, with no request/trace ID a client could report back:
{ "error": "Internal server error" }
practices.solution:
{ "error": "Internal server error", "traceId": "a1b2c3d4-..." }
// Also included as a response header (e.g. X-Trace-Id), matching the ID used in server-side structured logs for that request
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: error response body/headers with no trace or correlation ID field, in an application with distributed tracing or structured logging already available

practices.title: Reusing a single DTO for both create and update operations despite differing field requirements
practices.description: A create operation typically forbids the client from supplying an ID (the server assigns it), while an update operation requires one
practices.risk: sharing one DTO class for both means either the ID field's required-ness can't be validated consistently, or the code has to add conditional, operation-aware validation logic that a dedicated DTO per operation would avoid entirely.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: the same DTO class used as the @RequestBody type for both a POST (create) and PUT/PATCH (update) endpoint on the same resource with genuinely different field requirements

practices.title: Not verifying consumer-driven API contracts before deploying breaking changes
practices.description: Without some form of contract testing (Pact, Spring Cloud Contract, or even a shared, versioned schema checked in CI) between an API's provider and its consumers, a change that looks harmless from the provider's side (renaming a field, tightening a validation rule) can silently break every consumer, discovered only when they start failing in production rather than caught before merge.
practices.risk: A change that looks harmless from the provider's side can silently break every consumer, discovered only when they start failing in production instead of being caught before merge.
practices.code:
// The order-service team renames a response field from "total" to "totalAmount" and ships it.
// No contract test catches this; the frontend and two downstream services all break simultaneously in production.
practices.solution:
// A Pact/Spring Cloud Contract test, generated from and verified against the consumer's actual expectations,
// runs in the order-service's CI pipeline and fails the build BEFORE the breaking field rename ships.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: CI pipeline for an API with multiple independent consumers with no consumer-driven contract verification step

practices.title: Inconsistent null vs field-omission convention in JSON responses
practices.description: If some fields with no value are serialized as null while others (perhaps due to differing Jackson inclusion settings on different DTOs) are omitted entirely from the JSON object, clients can't apply one consistent rule ('check for null' vs 'check if the key exists') across the whole API, and strongly-typed client languages in particular can behave very differently depending on which convention a given response happens to follow.
practices.risk: Clients can't apply one consistent rule across the API, and strongly-typed client languages behave very differently depending on which convention a given response happens to follow.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: some JSON responses in the API using explicit null for absent data while others omit the key entirely, with no shared documented convention

practices.title: Using GET requests with side effects
practices.description: GET is defined by HTTP semantics as safe (no side effects) and idempotent
practices.risk: a GET endpoint that mutates state (increments a counter, deletes a record, sends an email) can be triggered unintentionally by browser prefetching, link crawlers, proxies, or automated retries, none of which expect GET to change anything.
practices.detectionPattern: @GetMapping\([^)]*\)\s*\n\s*(?:public\s+)?[\w<>\[\]]+\s+\w+\([^)]*\)\s*\{(?:(?!\}).)*?\.(?:save|update|delete|cancel|remove)\(

practices.title: Not handling Content-Type/Accept negotiation explicitly, causing unexpected 406/415 errors
practices.description: If a client sends an unexpected (but reasonable) Content-Type or Accept header and the controller's produces/consumes attributes are too narrowly or inconsistently specified, Spring returns a 406 Not Acceptable or 415 Unsupported Media Type with a generic error page, confusing clients who don't understand why a seemingly valid request was rejected.
practices.risk: Clients don't understand why a seemingly valid request was rejected, since the response is a generic error page with no indication of what content type was actually expected.
practices.code:
@PostMapping(value = "/orders") // no explicit consumes/produces — behavior depends entirely on default configuration and can surprise clients
public Order createOrder(@RequestBody OrderRequest req) { ... }
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: controller with no explicit consumes/produces attributes, causing unexpected 406/415 errors for reasonable client requests

practices.title: Ignoring idempotency for POST endpoints that should be safe to retry
practices.description: Network failures mean clients sometimes can't tell whether a request actually reached the server before the connection dropped
practices.risk: they retry; a POST endpoint with a real-world side effect (creating a payment, sending an order) and no idempotency mechanism processes that retry as a brand-new, separate operation, potentially charging a customer twice or creating duplicate orders.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: POST endpoint performing a financially or otherwise consequentially significant, non-idempotent operation with no idempotency-key mechanism

practices.title: Using PUT for partial updates instead of PATCH
practices.description: PUT is conventionally understood as a full replacement of the resource
practices.risk: a PUT handler that treats its request body as a partial update (only applying the fields present) invites callers to send a full representation and then be confused when fields they omitted got wiped out to null/default, because the server's actual behavior doesn't match PUT's expected semantics.

practices.title: Not validating path variable format/type explicitly
practices.description: A @PathVariable Long id automatically returns a 400 for a non-numeric value
practices.risk: the default message is generic and unhelpful ('Failed to convert value of type java.lang.String'); for path variables with more specific format requirements (a UUID, a specific ID pattern), leaving validation entirely to type conversion misses the chance to give a clear, specific error before it hits deeper logic.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: @PathVariable value parsed/converted (UUID.fromString(), custom parsing) inside the controller/service body with no upfront format validation

practices.title: Conflicting status codes between @ResponseStatus on an exception class and an @ExceptionHandler for the same exception
practices.description: If an exception class is annotated @ResponseStatus(NOT_FOUND) but a @ControllerAdvice also has an @ExceptionHandler for that same exception type returning a different status, the actual behavior depends on Spring's resolution precedence rules rather than either author's clear intent
practices.risk: the real status code a matter of implementation detail nobody explicitly decided.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: an exception class carrying @ResponseStatus while a @ControllerAdvice/@ExceptionHandler elsewhere also handles the same exception type with a different status code

practices.title: Custom servlet filters interfering with CORS preflight handling
practices.description: A hand-written filter that runs security/auth checks before Spring's CORS handling can process an OPTIONS preflight request will reject that preflight (since it typically carries no auth token), causing the browser to block the actual request entirely
practices.risk: even though the real request, if it had been allowed through, might have succeeded.
practices.detectionPattern: doFilter\([^)]*\)\s*\{(?:(?!\"OPTIONS\")(?!\}).)*?(?:isAuthenticated|sendError)\(

practices.title: Not specifying a default, deterministic sort order for list endpoints
practices.description: A query with no ORDER BY clause has no guaranteed row order from the database's perspective
practices.risk: a list endpoint that doesn't apply a default sort can return results in a different order between otherwise-identical requests (especially across pagination pages), causing items to appear duplicated or missing as a client pages through results.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_ANNOTATION_HEURISTIC: Pageable-based list endpoint parameter with no @PageableDefault sort specified

practices.title: Using HttpSession/@SessionAttributes in an otherwise stateless REST API
practices.description: REST APIs are conventionally stateless
practices.risk: each request carries everything needed to process it (typically via a token), which is exactly what lets them scale horizontally behind a load balancer with no session affinity required. Storing per-user state in HttpSession reintroduces server-side session state, forcing sticky sessions or shared session storage just to keep working across multiple instances.
practices.detectionPattern: HttpSession\s+\w+\)|@SessionAttributes\(

practices.title: Manually streaming a response body without setting correct Content-Length/Transfer-Encoding
practices.description: Writing directly to the response's OutputStream without either setting an accurate Content-Length upfront or properly using chunked Transfer-Encoding can cause clients to hang waiting for more data (if the client expects a specific length that never arrives) or truncate the response early.
practices.risk: Clients can hang waiting for more data that never arrives, or the response gets truncated early, depending on framework/container-specific defaults nobody explicitly chose.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: manual HttpServletResponse.getOutputStream() usage for a large/streamed response with no explicit Content-Length or chunked Transfer-Encoding configuration

practices.title: Not setting a timeout on async controller methods
practices.description: A controller method returning DeferredResult, Callable, or WebAsyncTask holds the underlying HTTP request open until it completes
practices.risk: with no timeout configured, a slow or stuck downstream dependency can leave that request (and the container thread capacity it ties up) hanging indefinitely, exactly the kind of unbounded wait a timeout exists to prevent.
practices.detectionPattern: new\s+DeferredResult<[^>]*>\(\s*\)

practices.title: Not setting an explicit charset on text-based media types
practices.description: Without an explicit charset in the produces/consumes media type (e.g. application/json;charset=UTF-8 rather than just application/json), the actual byte encoding used can vary by platform/configuration default, causing non-ASCII characters (accented letters, non-Latin scripts, emoji) to be mis-decoded on either end of the exchange.
practices.risk: Non-ASCII characters can be mis-decoded on either end of the exchange because the actual byte encoding used is left to platform-specific defaults.
practices.code:
@GetMapping(value = "/greeting", produces = "text/plain") // no charset specified — encoding is left to defaults, which may differ across environments
public String greeting() { return "caf\u00e9"; } // non-ASCII character, encoding now ambiguous
practices.solution:
@GetMapping(value = "/greeting", produces = "text/plain;charset=UTF-8") // explicit, unambiguous encoding
public String greeting() { return "caf\u00e9"; }
practices.detectionPattern: produces\s*=\s*\"(?:text/plain|text/csv|application/json)(?!;charset)[^\"]*\"

practices.title: Applying validation to request bodies but not to query parameters
practices.description: A @Valid @RequestBody DTO gets full Bean Validation coverage
practices.risk: a sibling @RequestParam or @PathVariable on the same or a similar endpoint often gets none at all unless @Validated is explicitly added at the class level with constraint annotations on the parameters themselves — an easy, inconsistent gap that lets malformed query input reach business logic unchecked while request bodies are protected.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_ANNOTATION_HEURISTIC: @RequestParam/@PathVariable with an obvious valid-range constraint but no @Validated at the class level and no constraint annotation on the parameter itself

practices.title: Serializing monetary values as JSON floating-point numbers
practices.description: JSON numbers are typically parsed as IEEE-754 doubles by many client languages/libraries
practices.risk: serializing a BigDecimal monetary amount as a plain JSON number risks precision loss on the client side (e.g. 19.999999999999996 instead of 20.00) even if the server-side value was perfectly precise, purely because of how the client's JSON parser represents numbers.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_ANNOTATION_HEURISTIC: BigDecimal-typed DTO field (not a JPA @Entity field, which is never directly serialized) representing money, serialized as a plain JSON number with no explicit string-based or scaled-integer strategy

practices.title: Not implementing pagination for list endpoints with unbounded result sets
practices.description: A list endpoint that returns 'all' matching records without limit works fine in testing with a handful of rows
practices.risk: as the underlying table grows, the same endpoint can eventually try to serialize and transmit millions of records in a single response, exhausting memory and network bandwidth for both server and client.

practices.title: Not setting Cache-Control/ETag headers for cacheable GET resources
practices.description: A GET endpoint serving data that rarely changes (reference data, a public catalog) but returning no caching headers forces every client and intermediary (CDN, browser, proxy) to re-fetch the full response every single time, wasting bandwidth and server load that a simple Cache-Control or ETag header could have avoided entirely.
practices.risk: Every client and intermediary has to re-fetch the full response every single time, wasting bandwidth and server load a simple header could have avoided entirely.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: GET endpoint serving infrequently-changing reference/catalog data with no Cache-Control, ETag, or Last-Modified header

practices.title: Not supporting conditional requests for expensive-to-generate resources
practices.description: Without ETag/If-None-Match support, a client that already has the current version of a resource still has to download the full response again to confirm nothing changed
practices.risk: conditional requests let the server respond with a cheap 304 Not Modified when the content is unchanged, saving both server computation and network transfer for expensive resources.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: GET endpoint for a computationally expensive or large resource with no ETag/If-None-Match conditional-request handling

practices.title: Forcing N individual API calls instead of providing a batch endpoint
practices.description: If a client routinely needs to fetch or update many individual resources by ID (e.g. 100 order statuses), and the API only offers a single-resource endpoint, the client is forced into N round-trips
practices.risk: each with its own latency, connection overhead, and failure mode — when one well-designed batch endpoint could satisfy the same need in a single call.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: client code calling a single-resource endpoint N times in a row for what is logically one batch operation, with no batch endpoint offered

practices.title: Using a wide-open, global CORS configuration
practices.description: @CrossOrigin("*") or an equivalent global CorsConfiguration allowing any origin removes the browser's same-origin protection entirely for that API, letting any website make authenticated cross-origin requests on behalf of a logged-in user (if cookies/credentials are also allowed)
practices.risk: a significant CSRF-adjacent exposure for anything beyond a fully public, unauthenticated API.
practices.detectionPattern: @CrossOrigin\([^)]*origins\s*=\s*\"\*\"|setAllowedOrigins\(\s*(?:List\.of|Arrays\.asList)\(\s*\"\*\"\s*\)\)

practices.title: Not implementing rate limiting on public-facing API endpoints
practices.description: Without any rate limiting, a single client (malicious or simply misbehaving due to a retry-loop bug) can send an unbounded volume of requests, degrading service for every other user and potentially exhausting downstream resources (database connections, third-party API quotas) that are shared across all traffic.
practices.risk: A single client can degrade service for every other user and exhaust downstream resources shared across all traffic.
practices.code:
@PostMapping("/login") // no rate limiting at all — vulnerable to brute-force attempts or simple retry-storm bugs from any single client
public ResponseEntity<?> login(@RequestBody LoginRequest req) { ... }
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: public, unauthenticated, or otherwise abuse-prone endpoint with no rate-limiting mechanism anywhere in the request path

practices.title: Leaving Spring Boot's default error handling exposing stack traces in production
practices.description: Spring Boot's default error attributes can include the exception's stack trace in the JSON error response if server.error.include-stacktrace is left at (or set to) 'always'
practices.risk: in production, this leaks internal implementation details (class names, line numbers, library versions) to any client that triggers an error.
practices.code:
server:
  error:
    include-stacktrace: always # exposes full stack traces in every error response, in every environment including production
practices.solution:
server:
  error:
    include-stacktrace: never # or 'on_param' scoped to trusted internal diagnostics only
    include-message: never # combined with a custom @ControllerAdvice for a clean, safe error contract
practices.detectionPattern: include-stacktrace:\s*always

practices.title: Returning DTOs that include sensitive internal fields via naive entity-to-DTO mapping
practices.description: Using a generic object mapper (or a naive manual mapper) that copies every field from an entity to a DTO by matching names can accidentally carry over sensitive fields
practices.risk: password hashes, internal audit columns, other users' foreign keys — into the public API response simply because the DTO happened to declare a same-named field for an unrelated reason.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_ANNOTATION_HEURISTIC: DTO field named identically to a sensitive entity field (password, secret, token) populated via a generic/reflection-based mapper rather than explicit field-by-field mapping

practices.title: Not enforcing a request body size limit
practices.description: Without an explicit maximum request size, a client (malicious or buggy) can send an arbitrarily large request body, forcing the server to buffer and attempt to process it
practices.risk: a cheap way to exhaust memory or bandwidth on the server side, especially against endpoints that don't otherwise need large payloads.
practices.code:
# No server.tomcat.max-http-form-post-size / spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size configured anywhere
# A client can POST a multi-gigabyte body to any endpoint with no server-side rejection
practices.solution:
server:
  tomcat:
    max-http-form-post-size: 2MB
spring:
  servlet:
    multipart:
      max-file-size: 10MB
      max-request-size: 10MB
# Explicit, sensible upper bounds appropriate to what each endpoint legitimately needs
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: application configuration with no explicit max request/file size settings for an API accepting bodies or uploads from untrusted clients

practices.title: Not controlling JSON serialization exposure via @JsonIgnore/@JsonProperty
practices.description: Without explicit control over which fields (and computed getters) get serialized, a DTO or entity can leak internal-only fields (a computed cache flag, an internal status enum ordinal, a bidirectional relationship back-reference) into the public API response simply because they happen to have a public getter Jackson picks up by convention.
practices.risk: A DTO or entity can leak internal-only fields into the public API response simply because they happen to have a public getter Jackson picks up by convention.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_ANNOTATION_HEURISTIC: public getter for a computed internal-only value serialized by Jackson with no @JsonIgnore

practices.title: Inconsistent authentication/authorization enforcement across sibling endpoints on the same resource
practices.description: If GET /orders/{id} requires authentication but DELETE /orders/{id} on the exact same resource was accidentally left unsecured (a missing @PreAuthorize, a gap in the security filter chain's path matching), an attacker can bypass the read protection entirely and go straight for the unprotected write operation.
practices.risk: An attacker can bypass the read protection entirely and go straight for the unprotected write operation on the exact same resource.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: a resource with some HTTP-method handlers carrying authorization annotations and sibling handlers on the same resource with none

practices.title: Trusting client-provided Content-Type/filename on file uploads without server-side validation
practices.description: The Content-Type header and original filename in a multipart upload are entirely client-controlled and easily spoofed
practices.risk: accepting them at face value to decide how to store or process a file (e.g. trusting 'image/png' to skip virus scanning, or using the raw filename as a storage path) lets an attacker upload disguised malicious content or manipulate storage paths.
practices.detectionPattern: \+\s*\w+\.getOriginalFilename\(\)

practices.title: Constructing file system paths from unsanitized path variables
practices.description: If a @PathVariable value is concatenated directly into a file system path with no validation, a request containing '../' sequences can escape the intended directory entirely, reading (or in a write endpoint, overwriting) arbitrary files elsewhere on the server's file system.
practices.risk: A request containing '../' sequences can escape the intended directory entirely, reading or overwriting arbitrary files elsewhere on the server's file system.

practices.title: Not validating actual file content against the claimed file type
practices.description: Checking only the file extension or the client-supplied Content-Type header to decide whether an uploaded file is 'safe' (e.g. an image) can be trivially bypassed by renaming a malicious executable to something.jpg
practices.risk: inspecting the file's actual magic bytes/content signature is the only way to verify what a file actually is, independent of what it claims to be.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_ANNOTATION_HEURISTIC: file upload handler validating type via getOriginalFilename()/getContentType() only, with no content-based magic-byte verification

practices.title: Ignoring the Vary header when responses differ by content negotiation
practices.description: If a single URL can return different representations depending on a request header (Accept-Language, Accept for content negotiation, an API-version header), an intermediary cache that doesn't know this
practices.risk: because the response never declared Vary — can serve one client's cached response (e.g. in French) to a different client that requested another language entirely, a form of cache poisoning caused purely by a missing header.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: cacheable endpoint whose response content varies by request header with no corresponding Vary header naming that header

practices.title: Missing Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite flags on cookies carrying session or auth tokens
practices.description: A cookie without Secure can be sent over plain HTTP if an attacker downgrades the connection
practices.risk: without HttpOnly, it's readable by JavaScript (and thus by an XSS payload); without an appropriate SameSite value, it can be sent along with cross-site requests, enabling CSRF. Omitting any of these on an authentication cookie removes a layer of defense with essentially no benefit.
practices.code: ResponseCookie cookie = ResponseCookie.from("session", token).build(); // no secure(), no httpOnly(), no sameSite() — all default to the least protective option
practices.solution:
ResponseCookie cookie = ResponseCookie.from("session", token)
    .httpOnly(true)
    .secure(true)
    .sameSite("Strict")
    .path("/")
    .maxAge(Duration.ofHours(1))
    .build();
practices.detectionPattern: ResponseCookie\.from\([^)]*\)(?![\s\S]{0,200}?\.httpOnly\(\s*true\s*\))

practices.title: N+1 query from a lazily-loaded association accessed in a loop
practices.description: Accessing a lazy @OneToMany/@ManyToOne inside a loop over the parent entities issues one extra query per row instead of a single joined/batched fetch.
practices.risk: A page that's fast with 10 test rows issues hundreds of queries against real data and times out or saturates the connection pool.
practices.solution:
@Query("SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.customer")
List<Order> findAllWithCustomer();
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: loop over a repository result accessing a lazy association's getter

practices.title: Loading an entire table into memory instead of paging
practices.description: findAll() with no Pageable pulls every row into memory and serializes all of it, regardless of what the caller actually needed.
practices.risk: Works in dev with 50 rows, then OOMs or produces a multi-second, multi-megabyte response once the table has millions.
practices.detectionPattern: findAll\(\)(?!.*Pageable)

practices.title: Missing @Version field allows lost updates
practices.description: Without optimistic locking, two concurrent updates to the same row both succeed, and the second silently overwrites the first's changes.
practices.risk: Two users editing the same order at once: one user's changes vanish with no error and no record that a conflict happened.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: @Entity class with mutable fields and no @Version

practices.title: SQL built via string concatenation
practices.description: Concatenating a user-controlled value into a SQL string is a SQL injection vector. A PreparedStatement with bound parameters is not optional here, even for internal tools.
practices.risk: An attacker-controlled userId value like `' OR '1'='1` returns every row in the table, or worse, chains into a destructive statement.

practices.title: Missing index on a frequently filtered or joined column
practices.description: A WHERE/JOIN on a column with no index forces a full table scan; the query gets slower in direct proportion to table size.
practices.risk: A query that returns in milliseconds on a 1,000-row dev table takes seconds on the 10-million-row production table, and locks up under concurrent load.
practices.solution:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id ON orders(customer_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders(status);
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: WHERE/JOIN column with no matching CREATE INDEX in the migration set

practices.title: Table charset not set to utf8mb4
practices.description: MySQL's utf8 charset is actually a 3-byte-max encoding and can't store emoji or many CJK/astral characters; utf8mb4 is the real UTF-8.
practices.risk: Saving a name or comment containing an emoji either throws an 'Incorrect string value' error or silently truncates the string at the offending character.
practices.detectionPattern: CHARSET\s*=\s*utf8(?!mb4)

practices.title: Comparing a VARCHAR column to a number causes an implicit cast and a full table scan
practices.description: MySQL implicitly converts types in a comparison. WHERE order_code = 12345 against a VARCHAR column silently casts every row's value instead of using the index.
practices.risk: A query that should hit an index on order_code instead scans the whole table, and this only shows up once the table is large enough to notice.
practices.code: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_code = 12345;
practices.solution: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_code = '12345';
practices.detectionPattern: WHERE\s+\w*code\w*\s*=\s*\d+(?!')

practices.title: Loose equality (==) instead of strict equality (===)
practices.description: == performs type coercion before comparing (0 == '' is true, null == undefined is true), producing comparisons that pass when they shouldn't.
practices.risk: A guard like `if (userId == 0)` also matches an empty string or false, letting an unintended branch execute for unexpected input shapes.

practices.title: var instead of let/const causing function-scoped leakage
practices.description: var is function-scoped and hoisted, so a variable declared inside a block (loop, if) leaks outside it and can be redeclared without error — unlike the block-scoped let/const.
practices.risk: A classic bug: a var loop counter captured in an async callback ends up with the same final value in every callback instead of each iteration's value.
practices.detectionPattern: \bvar\s+\w+

practices.title: Using any to silence a type error instead of typing the value
practices.description: any opts a value out of type checking entirely, so a typo'd property name or wrong argument type compiles cleanly and fails only at runtime.
practices.risk: A refactor that renames a field breaks every `any`-typed call site silently at compile time; the failure only shows up when that code path runs.
practices.detectionPattern: :\s*any\b

practices.title: Mutating state directly instead of via the state setter
practices.description: React decides whether to re-render by comparing references. Mutating an array/object in place keeps the same reference, so React doesn't know anything changed.
practices.risk: The UI silently stops reflecting the actual data — an item added to a list never appears until some unrelated state change forces a re-render.
practices.detectionPattern: \w+\.(push|splice|pop|shift|unshift)\([^)]*\)\s*;\s*set\w+\(

practices.title: dangerouslySetInnerHTML with unsanitized content
practices.description: Rendering raw HTML from an untrusted source (user input, an external API) without sanitizing it first is a stored/reflected XSS vector.
practices.risk: A user-submitted comment containing a <script> tag executes in every other visitor's browser session, with access to their cookies/tokens.
practices.code: <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: comment.body }} />
practices.solution:
import DOMPurify from 'dompurify';

<div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: DOMPurify.sanitize(comment.body) }} />
practices.detectionPattern: dangerouslySetInnerHTML

practices.title: Inline function/object literal passed as a prop defeats React.memo
practices.description: A new function or object literal is created on every render. Passed to a React.memo'd child, it breaks the prop-equality check that memo relies on, so the child re-renders anyway.
practices.risk: A list of memoized rows re-renders on every parent state change regardless of the memoization, and nobody notices why the optimization isn't working.
practices.code: <MemoizedRow onSelect={() => handleSelect(item.id)} style={{ padding: 8 }} />

practices.title: Non-semantic clickable div instead of a button element
practices.description: A <div onClick> gets none of a <button>'s built-in keyboard focus, Enter/Space activation, or screen-reader role for free — all of it has to be reimplemented by hand, and usually isn't.
practices.risk: A keyboard-only or screen-reader user cannot activate the control at all; it's invisible to assistive technology as an interactive element.
practices.code: Submit
practices.solution: <button type="button" className="submit-btn" onClick={handleSubmit}>Submit</button>
practices.detectionPattern: <div[^>]*onClick

practices.title: Image missing alt text
practices.description: An with no alt attribute is announced by a screen reader as just the filename, or skipped entirely, conveying nothing about its content or purpose.
practices.risk: A screen-reader user gets no information about a meaningful image (a chart, a product photo) and may miss content sighted users rely on.

practices.title: Overusing !important instead of fixing selector specificity
practices.description: !important overrides normal cascade rules and compounds: once one rule needs it to win, the next override needs !important too, and the cascade becomes unpredictable.
practices.risk: A later, more specific rule that should win silently loses to an unrelated !important declared months earlier, and the fix is to add yet another !important.
practices.detectionPattern: !important

practices.title: Hardcoded magic-number colors/spacing instead of design tokens
practices.description: A literal hex color or pixel value repeated across many rules means a design change requires a find-and-replace across the whole codebase instead of one variable update.
practices.risk: A brand color update or a spacing-scale change requires touching dozens of files, and it's easy to miss one, leaving a visibly inconsistent UI.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: repeated literal color/spacing value across multiple rules with no custom property

practices.title: Overriding Bootstrap classes with inline !important instead of Sass variable overrides
practices.description: Patching Bootstrap's look with scattered inline !important styles fights the framework instead of configuring it, and breaks the next time Bootstrap is upgraded.
practices.risk: A Bootstrap version bump changes a selector's specificity and the !important overrides stop applying in some places but not others, producing inconsistent styling that's hard to trace.
practices.code: <button class="btn btn-primary" style="background-color: #123456 !important;">Save</button>
practices.detectionPattern: style="[^"]*!important

practices.title: Hardcoding pixel breakpoints instead of Bootstrap's responsive grid/utilities
practices.description: A custom @media (max-width: 800px) duplicates logic Bootstrap's grid and responsive utility classes (col-md-*, d-none d-md-block) already provide consistently across the app.
practices.risk: Every hand-rolled breakpoint is a slightly different number, so the app's responsive behavior becomes inconsistent page to page, and Bootstrap's own components break out of sync with the custom ones.
practices.solution: ...
practices.detectionPattern: @media\s*\(max-width:\s*\d+px\)

practices.title: Hardcoded credential or API key in source
practices.description: A committed secret is compromised the moment it's pushed, whether or not the repo is public today — history doesn't forget. Load secrets from environment/config at runtime instead.
practices.risk: Anyone with read access to the repo (or its history, even after a later 'fix') can extract and use the credential; rotation is the only real remediation once this happens.
practices.code: String apiKey = "sk-live-91a2b3c4d5e6f7g8h9i0";
practices.solution: String apiKey = System.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY");
practices.detectionPattern: (password|apiKey|secret|token)\s*=\s*"[^"]{8,}"

practices.title: API key or secret embedded in a frontend bundle
practices.description: Anything shipped in client-side JavaScript is visible to every visitor via browser devtools, regardless of minification. A frontend can only safely hold public, purpose-limited keys.
practices.risk: A backend-scoped API key embedded for convenience gets extracted from the bundle and used directly against the provider, outside any of the app's own rate limits or authorization checks.
practices.code:
const OPENAI_KEY = "sk-live-91a2b3c4d5e6f7g8h9i0";
fetch("https://api.openai.com/v1/...", { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${OPENAI_KEY}` } });
practices.solution:
// Call your own backend, which holds the real key server-side.
fetch("/api/reviews", { method: "POST", body });
practices.detectionPattern: (sk-|ghp_|AKIA)[A-Za-z0-9]{10,}

practices.title: Logging sensitive data
practices.description: Passwords, tokens, and full card numbers written to logs end up in log aggregators, backups, and support tickets — systems with far weaker access control than the original request.
practices.risk: A support engineer or a compromised log-aggregation account gets direct access to live credentials, without ever touching the production database.
practices.code: log.info("Login attempt: user={} password={}", username, password);
practices.solution: log.info("Login attempt: user={}", username);
practices.detectionPattern: log\.\w+\([^)]*password[^)]*\)

practices.title: Adding a dependency without pinning a version or verifying the package name
practices.description: An unpinned version range can pull in a breaking or malicious update on the next build; a mistyped package name can pull in an unrelated (or malicious, typosquatted) package entirely.
practices.risk: A typosquatted package (e.g. `reqeusts` instead of `requests`) runs arbitrary code at install time; an unpinned range silently upgrades into a breaking API change on the next clean install.
practices.code: "some-utility": "*"
practices.solution: "some-utility": "^2.3.1"  // verified on npmjs.com: correct name, real maintainers, matches expected download counts
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: dependency manifest entry with a wildcard/unbounded version range

practices.title: Test with no assertions
practices.description: A test that only calls the method under test and returns proves the code doesn't throw — nothing about whether it did the right thing. It stays green through real regressions.
practices.risk: A genuine regression in business logic ships to production with full test coverage reported green, because the test never actually checked the outcome.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_ASSERTION_HEURISTIC: method annotated @Test whose body contains no assert*/verify* call
